  3. Creating Interactive Dashboards: Drag visuals onto the canvas to build your dashboard.
  4. DAX Basics: DAX stands for Data Analysis Expressions.
  5. Sharing Reports: Publish dashboards to Power BI Service.
  6. Power BI Service & Cloud: Power BI Service is the online platform for sharing and collaboration.
  7. Practical: Build a Business Dashboard: Choose a dataset related to business (e.g., sales, finance, operations).
  8. Power BI Project: Choose a business dataset and build a dashboard in Power BI.
⭐ Activity: Close the lesson. Say each point above out loud in your own words, then give one example from your own life or work. Any point you cannot explain is where to go back and re-read.
Recall round (answer before you look)

Cover the answers. Say or write your answer to each question, then check yourself in the last layer below.

  1. Why do professionals spend most of their Power BI time before building any visual? (from: Power BI Overview)
  2. What is the difference between a calculated column and a measure? (from: Data Modeling in Power BI)
  3. Why use <code>DIVIDE([Total Sales],[Orders])</code> instead of <code>[Total Sales]/[Orders]</code>? (from: DAX Basics)
  4. A manager should see only their own branch numbers. What feature handles this? (from: Sharing Reports)
  5. For a clinic dashboard, why should you show aggregated visits rather than patient names? (from: Real-World Use Cases)
  6. What three parts belong in a good dashboard summary? (from: Power BI Project)
Teach it back
  1. Explain the three ideas you find hardest to a friend or family member in two minutes, without notes.
  2. Wherever you stumble, write the lesson name down and go back to it. Re-read the Practice layer and redo the activity.
  3. This week, use one idea from this module in real life or work, and note what happened.
  4. Come back in two days and answer the recall questions again. Remembering after a gap is what makes it stay.

Lessons to revisit if needed:

  • Power BI Overview
  • Connecting to Multiple Data Sources
  • Creating Interactive Dashboards
  • DAX Basics
  • Sharing Reports
  • Power BI Service & Cloud
  • Practical: Build a Business Dashboard
  • Power BI Project
Check yourself: the answers

Answers, in the same order:

  1. Because visuals rely on clean, well-modelled data. Wrong types, duplicates or bad relationships give wrong numbers on any chart.
  2. A calculated column is computed per row and stored in the model. A measure is computed when the visual needs it, responds to filters and uses less memory.
  3. DIVIDE returns blank (or an alternative you choose) when the denominator is zero, so you avoid divide-by-zero errors in visuals.
  4. Row-level security: define roles with a filter on branch in the model, then assign users to the role in the Service.
  5. Aggregates answer management questions and protect patient privacy. Personal identifiers are rarely needed for performance tracking and create risk if shared.
  6. The finding, the evidence from the visuals, and a suggested action or next question.

slides.title: Start with a tiny program
slides.content:
Today you will make the computer display one line. You do not need to understand everything yet. A program is a set of instructions that the computer follows in order.

print("Hello, world!")
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkWhat does print("Hello, world!") do?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Open Python IDLE if Python is installed. On Windows, open Start, type IDLE, and open Python 3.x IDLE. If IDLE is unavailable, use the Python editor already approved by your teacher; do not download unknown software.
  2. In IDLE choose File, then New File. A blank editor window opens.
  3. Type exactly: print("Hello, world!"). The brackets and quotation marks matter.
  4. Choose Run, then Run Module (or press F5). If asked to save, save as first_program.py.
  5. Look at the Shell window. You should see Hello, world!
  6. Change the words inside the quotes to your name, save, and run again.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

The file ending .py tells you it is a Python source file. The editor is where you write instructions; the Shell is where you see output and errors.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: What appeared in the Shell after you ran the program? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Instructions happen in order
slides.content:
A computer does not guess what you mean. It follows instructions one at a time, from top to bottom. A good set of instructions is clear and in the right order.

print("Step 1: Open the notebook")
print("Step 2: Write the date")
print("Step 3: Save your work")
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkA program has three print lines. In what order does Python follow them?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Open your first_program.py file again, or create a new file.
  2. Type the three print lines exactly as shown, one line at a time.
  3. Run the program. Read the output from top to bottom.
  4. Move the third line to the top. Run it again and notice that the computer follows the new order.
  5. Write three instructions for making tea or opening a shop. Put them in the order they should happen.
  6. Turn each instruction into a print line and run it.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

The written plan is an algorithm: a finite set of steps for completing a task. Code is one way to express those steps in a language a computer can run.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: If you move a print line to a different position, what changes? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Display words with print()
slides.content:
print() tells Python to display something. The word print is followed by parentheses. Put text inside quotation marks between the parentheses.

print("Good morning")
print("Today I am learning Python")
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkWhich line is written correctly?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Create a new file and type the first line exactly.
  2. Notice the opening parenthesis immediately after print and the closing parenthesis at the end.
  3. Notice that the message begins and ends with matching quotation marks.
  4. Run the file. You should see Good morning.
  5. Add a second print line and run again.
  6. Change the message. Then deliberately remove the final quotation mark and run. Read the error, restore the quotation mark, and run again.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

Python is case-sensitive: print() works, but Print() is a different name and will fail unless you define it. Parentheses group the value being passed to print. Straight quotation marks are safest when typing code.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: Which two punctuation marks surround the message passed to print()? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Store information in variables
slides.content:
A variable is a name that refers to a value. Think of it as a labelled box. The equals sign = assigns a value to the name; it does not mean 'is equal to' in a maths question.

name = "Amina"
age = 20
print(name)
print(age)
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkAfter age = 20, what does print(age) show?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type name = "Amina" on the first line. Keep the quotation marks around the name because it is text.
  2. On the next line type age = 20. This is a whole number, so it has no quotation marks.
  3. On the next two lines type print(name) and print(age). Notice that the variable names themselves are not inside quotes.
  4. Run the program and check that Amina and 20 appear.
  5. Change the name and age to different values and run again.
  6. Try changing name to Name in print(Name). Run it, read the error, then correct the capital letter.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

Variable names may use letters, digits and underscores, but cannot start with a digit or contain spaces. Python treats name and Name as different names. Use descriptive names such as monthly_sales rather than x when the meaning matters.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: In print(name), why are there no quotation marks around name? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Text and numbers are different
slides.content:
Text is called a string and is written inside quotes. Numbers can be stored as integers (whole numbers) or floats (numbers with a decimal point). Python handles them differently.

shop = "12"
items = 12
print(shop)
print(items + 3)
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkWhich of these is text (a string)?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type shop = "12" and items = 12 on separate lines.
  2. Print both values. They may look similar on screen, but one is text and one is a number.
  3. Add print(items + 3). Run the file; the result should be 15.
  4. Now replace items with shop in that calculation: print(shop + 3). Run it and read the TypeError.
  5. Restore the working calculation. Explain in your notebook why the two values behave differently.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

A string can contain digits but is still text. An integer supports arithmetic. A float can store decimal values such as 125.50. Do not use a rounded or simplified example as a substitute for accurate financial records.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: Why does items + 3 work while shop + 3 causes an error? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Use Python as a calculator
slides.content:
Python can perform arithmetic. Use + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication and / for division. The order of operations still matters.

sales = 1500
costs = 950
profit = sales - costs
print(profit)
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkWhat does 2 + 3 * 4 give?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type the four lines exactly. A variable stores sales, another stores costs, and profit stores the result.
  2. Run the program. You should see 550.
  3. Change sales to 2000 and costs to 1250. Run it again.
  4. Add print(sales + costs) to see addition.
  5. Try print(10 * 4) and print(20 / 5) on separate lines.
  6. Try print(2 + 3 * 4), then print((2 + 3) * 4). Compare the results.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

Python follows operator precedence: multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction. Parentheses make the intended order clear. Division with / produces a decimal result, even when the answer is a whole number.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: What is the difference between 2 + 3 * 4 and (2 + 3) * 4? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Ask the user for information
slides.content:
input() pauses the program and waits for the user to type an answer. The answer is returned as text. You can store it in a variable and display it later.

name = input("What is your name? " )
print("Hello, " + name)
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkWhat kind of value does input() give back?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Create a new file and type the two lines exactly.
  2. Run the program. When the question appears, type your first name and press Enter.
  3. Check that the program greets you.
  4. Change the question to ask for your town. Change the greeting to use the town variable.
  5. Try running the program and pressing Enter without typing anything. Notice what happens.
  6. Add a second input line to ask for a favourite food, then print the answer.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

input() returns a string. The + operator joins strings when both sides are text. The space inside "Hello, " makes the greeting easier to read.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: What does input() return: a number automatically, or text? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Turn typed digits into a number
slides.content:
Even when a user types 25, input() receives the characters as text. Use int() to convert text containing a whole number into an integer before doing arithmetic.

age_text = input("How old are you? " )
age = int(age_text)
print(age + 1)
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkA user types 25. Which line turns that text into a whole number?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type the three lines exactly and run the program.
  2. When asked for your age, type a whole number such as 20 and press Enter.
  3. Check that the program displays your age plus one.
  4. Replace int with float and try a decimal such as 20.5.
  5. Change the answer to a word such as twenty. Run it and read the ValueError.
  6. Restore the example and remember: int() expects text that represents a whole number.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

int('25') becomes 25. float('25.5') becomes 25.5. Conversion can fail if the user types letters or an invalid value. Real applications should validate input and explain what the user needs to enter.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: Why do we use int() around the value returned by input()? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Make a decision with if and else
slides.content:
Programs can choose what to do. An if statement checks a condition. If it is true, its indented block runs. Otherwise, the else block runs.

cash = 800
if cash >= 500:
    print("You can cover the target")
else:
    print("You are below the target")
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkWhich symbol checks whether two values are equal?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type the example carefully. The colon : at the end of the if line is required.
  2. The two print lines begin with four spaces. This indentation shows which instructions belong to each branch.
  3. Run the program with cash = 800. Read the message.
  4. Change cash to 300 and run again.
  5. Change >= to > and test cash = 500. Compare the result.
  6. Try removing the colon or the indentation, run the program, and read the error. Then restore both.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

Comparison operators include == (equal to), != (not equal to), >, <, >= and <=. A single = assigns a value; a double == compares two values. Python uses indentation to define code blocks.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: What is the difference between = and == in Python? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Repeat work with a loop
slides.content:
A loop repeats instructions. Use a for loop when you know what values you want to go through. range(1, 4) produces 1, 2 and 3; the stop value 4 is not included.

for day in range(1, 4):
    print("Day", day)
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkHow many times does for day in range(1, 4): repeat?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type the two lines exactly. Notice the colon at the end of the for line.
  2. Indent the print line by four spaces. It belongs inside the loop.
  3. Run the program. You should see Day 1, Day 2 and Day 3.
  4. Change range(1, 4) to range(1, 6) and run again.
  5. Change the print message to print("Practising", day).
  6. Remove the indentation from print, run the program, and observe the difference or error. Restore the indentation.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

range(start, stop) includes start and excludes stop. A loop variable such as day takes each value in turn. Indentation determines which statements repeat.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: How many times does range(1, 6) repeat the loop? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Keep several values in a list
slides.content:
A list stores multiple values under one name. Each item has a position called an index. Python starts counting list positions at zero.

items = ["bread", "milk", "eggs"]
print(items[0])
print(items[1])
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkitems = ['bread', 'milk', 'eggs']. What is items[1]?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type the list exactly, including square brackets and commas between items.
  2. Run the two print lines. The first should display bread and the second milk.
  3. Add print(items[2]) to display eggs.
  4. Change milk to rice and run again.
  5. Try print(items[3]). Read the IndexError, then remove that line.
  6. Add a fourth item to the list and print it using its correct index.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

Lists use square brackets. Commas separate items. Index 0 means the first item, index 1 the second, and so on. len(items) tells you how many items are in a list.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: What index is used to access the first item in a Python list? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Create and use a function
slides.content:
A function is a named group of instructions. You define it with def, then call its name to make it run. The colon and indentation are important.

def greet():
    print("Welcome to the shop")

greet()
greet()
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkWhat makes a function run?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type def greet(): on the first line, including the colon.
  2. On the next line, indent by four spaces and type the print instruction.
  3. Leave a blank line, then type greet() twice.
  4. Run the program. The message should appear two times.
  5. Change the message and run again.
  6. Remove one call to greet() and run. Notice that defining a function does not automatically run it.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

The lines indented under def form the function body. A function can be called many times, which avoids copying the same instructions repeatedly. Later, functions can accept inputs called parameters and return results.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: What is the difference between defining greet() and calling greet()? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Read and fix an error
slides.content:
An error is information that helps you find a problem. Read the final line of the error message, then inspect the file name and line number. Do not panic or randomly change many lines.

price = 100
quantity = 3
total = price * quantity
print(totla)
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkPython says NameError: name 'totla' is not defined. What is the most likely cause?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Type the four lines exactly, including the misspelling totla in the last line.
  2. Run the program. Python should report a NameError because totla has not been defined.
  3. Read the error message. Find the line number it identifies.
  4. Compare the spelling in print(totla) with the variable total above it.
  5. Correct totla to total and run again. The result should be 300.
  6. In your notebook write: error, clue, cause, fix. Use those four words to explain what you did.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

Common beginner errors include SyntaxError (Python cannot understand the code), NameError (a name is not defined), TypeError (an operation uses incompatible types), ValueError (a value cannot be converted as requested) and IndentationError (spacing is inconsistent).

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: Which clue helped you fix the NameError in this exercise? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Build a simple shop calculator
slides.content:
Now combine variables, input, number conversion, arithmetic and if/else. This practice calculator compares sales with costs and reports whether the simple result is positive, zero or negative. It is a learning exercise, not a complete accounting system.

sales = float(input("Enter total sales: "))
costs = float(input("Enter total costs: "))
result = sales - costs
print("Result:", result)
if result > 0:
    print("Positive result")
elif result == 0:
    print("Break-even")
else:
    print("Negative result")
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkIn the shop calculator, which line finds the difference between sales and costs?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Create a new file and type the code line by line. Pay attention to the quotation marks, parentheses and colons.
  2. Indent the print lines under if, elif and else by four spaces each.
  3. Run the program. Enter sales of 15000 and costs of 12000. Check the result.
  4. Run it again with sales 10000 and costs 12000. Check the negative result.
  5. Run it a third time with sales 12000 and costs 12000. Check the break-even message.
  6. Change the output label from Result to Difference. Save the file.
  7. Explain each line aloud: input, conversion, subtraction, display and decision.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

elif means 'else if' and lets you test another condition when the earlier condition was false. For real business reporting, define whether costs include stock purchases, wages, tax, debt, timing differences and other items before calling a figure profit. This small program does not make those accounting decisions.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: Which line calculates the difference between sales and costs? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Use AI as a learning assistant
slides.content:
AI can explain code, suggest practice and help you understand an error. You must still type, run, test and explain the code yourself. Do not paste passwords, private customer records, patient information or confidential workplace data into an AI tool.

# Ask for an explanation, not a finished assignment
# Example prompt to use with an AI assistant:
# Explain this Python line in very simple steps: total = price * quantity
# Give me one small practice question. Do not write the answer yet.
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkAI suggests a code change. What should you do next?
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Choose one code line from a lesson you have completed.
  2. Ask an AI assistant: Explain this line in simple words, one symbol at a time.
  3. Ask: Give me one similar practice question, but do not show the answer.
  4. Attempt the question yourself in your editor and run it.
  5. If you get an error, share only the small non-confidential code sample and the error message.
  6. Ask for a hint first. Try the correction yourself before asking for a full explanation.
  7. Close the AI response and explain the code in your own words.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

Useful prompts include: 'Explain the colon in this if statement'; 'Give me a hint, not the solution'; 'Quiz me on variables'; and 'Review my attempt and point out one mistake at a time'. AI can be wrong, so verify suggestions by running small tests and checking trusted documentation.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: What should you do after AI suggests a code change? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Independent practice challenge
slides.content:
This is your check that you can write small programs without copying every line. Try at least three tasks. Use your notes only after making a genuine attempt.

# Task 1
print("My first independent program")

# Task 2
a = 8
b = 5
print(a + b)
Do it now: Type the example yourself, run it, and compare your result with the expected behaviour. Do not only read the code.
Concept checkYou are ready to move on when you can...
Step-by-step layer

Follow these steps in order. Keep your editor open while you practise.

  1. Task 1: Write a program that displays a greeting of your choice.
  2. Task 2: Create two number variables and display their sum.
  3. Task 3: Ask the user for a name and display a greeting using that name.
  4. Task 4: Ask for a whole number. Convert it with int(). If it is at least 10, display '10 or more'; otherwise display 'Below 10'.
  5. Task 5: Use a for loop to display the numbers 1 to 5.
  6. Choose at least three tasks. Type each solution yourself, save it, and run it.
  7. For each task, change one value or message and run it again.
  8. Explain the role of every punctuation mark you used: quotes, brackets, parentheses, commas, colons and indentation.

Before moving on: Save your work. If the result is different, read the error message and check spelling, punctuation and indentation before trying again.

Power-user layer

You are ready to move on when you can create, run, modify and explain a small program; recognise a basic error; and find the line that needs attention. If you cannot yet do that, repeat the matching lesson. Speed is not the goal; understanding is.

Good habit: Change one thing at a time, run the program again, and record what changed. This makes cause and effect easier to understand.

Check yourself

Self-check: Which task did you complete without copying, and what did you learn from it? Write or say your answer in your own words. If you are unsure, repeat the step-by-step activity before continuing.

slides.title: Lock It In: Module Recap
slides.content:
1. Start with a tiny program: Today you will make the computer display one line. You do not need to understand everything yet. A program is a set of instructions that the computer follows in order.
  2. Display words with print(): print() tells Python to display something. The word print is followed by parentheses. Put text inside quotation marks between the parentheses.
  3. Text and numbers are different: Text is called a string and is written inside quotes. Numbers can be stored as integers (whole numbers) or floats (numbers with a decimal point). Python handles them differently.
  4. Ask the user for information: input() pauses the program and waits for the user to type an answer. The answer is returned as text. You can store it in a variable and display it later.
  5. Repeat work with a loop: A loop repeats instructions. Use a for loop when you know what values you want to go through. range(1, 4) produces 1, 2 and 3; the stop value 4 is not included.
  6. Create and use a function: A function is a named group of instructions. You define it with def, then call its name to make it run. The colon and indentation are important.
  7. Build a simple shop calculator: Now combine variables, input, number conversion, arithmetic and if/else. This practice calculator compares sales with costs and reports whether the simple result is positive, zero or negative.
  8. Independent practice challenge: This is your check that you can write small programs without copying every line. Try at least three tasks. Use your notes only after making a genuine attempt.
⭐ Activity: Close the lesson. Say each point above out loud in your own words, then give one example from your own life or work. Any point you cannot explain is where to go back and re-read.
Concept checkWhat does print("Hello, world!") do?
Concept checkYou are ready to move on when you can...
Recall round (answer before you look)

Cover the answers. Say or write your answer to each question, then check yourself in the last layer below.

  1. What appeared in the Shell after you ran the program? (from: Start with a tiny program)
  2. In print(name), why are there no quotation marks around name? (from: Store information in variables)
  3. What does input() return: a number automatically, or text? (from: Ask the user for information)
  4. How many times does range(1, 6) repeat the loop? (from: Repeat work with a loop)
  5. Which clue helped you fix the NameError in this exercise? (from: Read and fix an error)
  6. Which task did you complete without copying, and what did you learn from it? (from: Independent practice challenge)
Teach it back
  1. Explain the three ideas you find hardest to a friend or family member in two minutes, without notes.
  2. Wherever you stumble, write the lesson name down and go back to it. Re-read the Practice layer and redo the activity.
  3. This week, use one idea from this module in real life or work, and note what happened.
  4. Come back in two days and answer the recall questions again. Remembering after a gap is what makes it stay.

Lessons to revisit if needed:

  • Start with a tiny program
  • Display words with print()
  • Text and numbers are different
  • Ask the user for information
  • Repeat work with a loop
  • Create and use a function
  • Build a simple shop calculator
  • Independent practice challenge
Check yourself: the answers

slides.title: Why Python for Data?
slides.content:
1. Python is a flexible, beginner-friendly programming language.
  2. It’s widely used in data science, machine learning, and automation.
  3. Python handles large datasets better than Excel.
  4. It has powerful libraries like pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn.
  5. You’ll use Python for cleaning, analysis, and visualization.
    6. Food for the Mind: “Python is your digital scalpel—precise, powerful, and ready to dissect data.”

Worked example: average sales by product

Sales file rows: Sugar 1,200; Sugar 800; Sugar 1,000; Milk 500; Milk 700.

  1. Load it: df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
  2. Group and average: df.groupby("Product")["Amount"].mean()
  3. Sugar: 1,200 + 800 + 1,000 = 3,000, then 3,000 / 3 = 1,000.
  4. Milk: 500 + 700 = 1,200, then 1,200 / 2 = 600.

Output shows Milk 600.0 and Sugar 1000.0.

Meaning: next month you change only the file name and rerun. The same steps run again in seconds, with no clicking to repeat.

Concept checkWanjiru must report average sales by product from a new sales file every month. Why might a pandas script suit this better than repeating Excel clicks?
Practitioner layer

Compare the same task in Excel and Python: average sales by product for 1 million rows.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
print(df.groupby("Product")["Amount"].mean())

Three lines, and rerunning on next month's file takes seconds. In Excel you would redo clicks each time. Python is also good for combining many files, cleaning text, and making charts. Excel remains great for quick looks and small ad-hoc work. The goal is not to replace Excel but to add a repeatable tool. Install steps come in the next slide.

Expert layer

Python's real advantage is repeatability and a written record of every step, which others can audit. Row limits in Excel are far larger than most small datasets, so do not abandon it for small tasks. Learn one library at a time: pandas first. Do not try to memorise syntax; keep a cheat sheet and search documentation. Read errors from the bottom line up. Next, set up Jupyter and run your first notebook.

Check yourself: Give one reason a script can beat repeating clicks in Excel each month.

Answer: A script repeats the same steps exactly on new data in seconds and leaves a written record of what was done, which reduces errors.

slides.title: Setting Up Python & Jupyter
slides.content:
1. Install Python from python.org or use Anaconda.
  2. Use Jupyter Notebook for writing and running code interactively.
  3. Install libraries using pip install pandas matplotlib seaborn.
  4. Notebooks let you mix code, notes, and visuals.
  5. Great for learning, experimenting, and sharing.
    6. Food for the Mind: “Jupyter is your lab—code, test, and learn in one place.”

Worked example: first setup on Windows

Hawa installs Python and wants to run her first cell.

  1. Open Command Prompt and run python --version. A version number appears, so Python is found.
  2. Run pip install pandas matplotlib seaborn jupyter while on Wi-Fi to save bundles.
  3. Run jupyter notebook. A browser tab opens.
  4. Choose New, then Python 3.
  5. In the first cell type print("Habari") and press Shift+Enter.

Result: Habari is printed under the cell.

Meaning: Python, pip and Jupyter all work together. Had step 1 shown "python is not recognized", she would reinstall with PATH ticked before going on.

Concept checkYou installed Python, but Command Prompt says "python is not recognized" when you type python --version. What is the best fix?
Practitioner layer

Set up on Windows.

  1. Install Python from python.org (tick "Add Python to PATH") or install Anaconda.
  2. Open Command Prompt and run python --version.
  3. Install libraries: pip install pandas matplotlib seaborn jupyter.
  4. Start Jupyter: jupyter notebook. A browser tab opens.
  5. Choose New, then Python 3, type print("Habari") and press Shift+Enter.

You should see Habari printed under the cell. If "python is not recognized", reinstall with PATH ticked or use the Anaconda Prompt. Free alternative: Google Colab runs notebooks in your browser with no install.

Expert layer

Use a virtual environment per project (python -m venv env) so library versions do not clash. Run cells in order; a notebook that works only in a certain execution order is a hidden bug, so periodically Restart and Run All. Keep each project in its own folder with the data beside the notebook. Save often. Data bundles are limited in cheap bundles, so install once while on Wi-Fi. Next, learn lists and dicts.

Check yourself: You typed <code>pip install pandas</code> and got "pip is not recognized". What is the likely fix?

Answer: Python is not on PATH. Reinstall with "Add Python to PATH" ticked, or use the Anaconda Prompt, then try again.

slides.title: Data Structures (lists, dicts, DataFrames)
slides.content:
1. list: ordered collection of items.
  2. dict: key-value pairs for structured data.
  3. DataFrame: table-like structure from pandas.
  4. Use df.head() to preview data.
  5. DataFrames are the heart of Python data analysis.
    6. Food for the Mind: “DataFrames are your spreadsheet in code—flexible, fast, and full of insight.”

The pandas lessons run in Jupyter on your own computer. This box lets you practise the pure-Python parts right here.

Open the full Playground

Worked example: list, dict and DataFrame

Mama Njeri tracks the same data in three shapes.

  1. List: sales = [1200, 800, 450]. sales[0] gives 1200 because counting starts at 0.
  2. Dict: shop = {"name": "Mama Njeri", "city": "Nakuru"}. shop["city"] gives Nakuru, picked by key.
  3. DataFrame: pd.DataFrame({"Product": ["Sugar", "Milk"], "Sales": [1200, 800]}) makes a two-row table.
  4. df["Sales"].sum() adds 1,200 + 800 = 2,000.

Meaning: use a list for ordered values, a dict for labelled facts and a DataFrame for a table you will analyse.

Concept checkGiven sales = [1200, 800, 450], what does print(sales[1]) show?
Practitioner layer

Same data, three shapes:

sales = [1200, 800, 450]                  # list
shop = {"name": "Mama Njeri", "city": "Nakuru"}   # dict
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"Product": ["Sugar", "Milk"], "Sales": [1200, 800]})
print(sales[0], shop["city"])
print(df.head())
print(df["Sales"].sum())

Output: 1200 Nakuru, then a two-row table, then 2000. Lists use positions starting at 0. Dicts use keys. A DataFrame is a table whose columns are Series. Use df.shape for rows and columns and df.dtypes for types.

Expert layer

Position counting from 0 trips every beginner. Square brackets mean different things: df["Sales"] picks a column, df[["Sales"]] returns a DataFrame. Avoid loops over rows when a column operation does the job; it is simpler and much faster. Learn df.loc[] for selecting rows by label or condition. Check df.dtypes early, since dates and numbers are often read as text. Next, read a real CSV.

Check yourself: What does <code>df["Sales"].sum()</code> do?

Answer: It selects the Sales column and adds up its values.

slides.title: Importing Data with pandas
slides.content:
1. import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df.head()
  2. Use read_csv() to load CSV files.
  3. Use read_excel() for Excel files.
  4. Preview data with head() and info().
  5. Check for missing values with isnull().sum().
  6. pandas makes importing fast and easy.
    7. Food for the Mind: “Importing is your handshake with the data—start clean, start smart.”

Worked example: load and inspect a CSV

data.csv has 4 rows. One row has a blank Amount.

  1. Load: df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
  2. df.head() shows up to 5 rows, so all 4 rows appear.
  3. df.info() lists the columns, types and non-null counts. Amount shows 3 non-null out of 4 entries.
  4. df.isnull().sum() counts blanks per column. Amount: 4 - 3 = 1.

Meaning: inspecting first reveals one missing Amount before any analysis. You can now decide how to handle it in code, while the raw file stays untouched.

Concept checkYour notebook runs pd.read_csv("data.csv") and shows FileNotFoundError. The file is in your Downloads folder, the notebook is in Documents. What should you do?
Practitioner layer

Load and inspect a CSV.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df.head()
df.info()
df.isnull().sum()
  1. Put data.csv in the notebook's folder.
  2. Run read_csv; for Excel use pd.read_excel("file.xlsx", sheet_name="Sales") (needs openpyxl).
  3. head() shows 5 rows; info() lists columns, types and non-null counts.
  4. isnull().sum() counts blanks per column.

If FileNotFoundError appears, check the file name and folder. For dates use parse_dates=["Date"].

Expert layer

Inspect before you trust. Look for wrong types, odd categories, blank rows and strange values. If you see UnicodeDecodeError, try encoding="latin-1". Large files can be read in pieces with chunksize. Do not edit the raw file: keep it untouched and do all cleaning in code so it is reproducible. Use relative paths so the notebook works on other machines. Never upload files with customer details to public tools. Next, clean the data.

Check yourself: <code>info()</code> shows Amount as "object" instead of a number. What does that suggest?

Answer: Some values in Amount are text (such as commas or symbols), so the column was read as strings. Clean it and convert with pd.to_numeric.

slides.title: Data Cleaning in pandas
slides.content:
1. df.dropna(inplace=True)
df['Name'] = df['Name'].str.strip().str.title()
df.drop_duplicates(inplace=True)
  2. Use dropna() to remove missing values.
  3. Use string functions to clean text.
  4. Use drop_duplicates() to remove repeats.
  5. Convert data types with astype() or to_datetime().
  6. Document your cleaning steps.
    7. Food for the Mind: “Cleaning with pandas is like brushing your data’s teeth—fresh, sharp, and ready to smile.”

Worked example: cleaning with row counts

customers.csv has 500 rows.

  1. Strip and title-case names. The row count stays 500.
  2. df = df.drop_duplicates() leaves 480. Removed: 500 - 480 = 20.
  3. pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") turns bad Amounts into NaN. Count first: df["Amount"].isnull().sum() gives 30.
  4. df = df.dropna(subset=["Amount"]) leaves 480 - 30 = 450.

Total removed: 20 + 30 = 50, and 500 - 450 = 50 agrees. That is 50 / 500 = 10%.

Meaning: comparing counts shows exactly what was lost. A 10% loss is worth a comment in the notebook.

Concept checkYou have 500 customer rows. After dropna() only 350 remain. What is the best next step?
Practitioner layer

A customer list with messy names.

df = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")
df["Name"] = df["Name"].str.strip().str.title()
df["Amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Amount"].str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], errors="coerce")
df = df.drop_duplicates()
df = df.dropna(subset=["Amount"])

" mama njeri " becomes "Mama Njeri"; "1,200" becomes 1200. Check with df.info() and df.duplicated().sum(). Write a comment on each step so a reader knows what you changed and why.

Expert layer

Dropping rows is a decision, not a default. Ask why values are missing; sometimes fill with a sensible value or keep and flag them instead. errors="coerce" turns bad values into NaN, so count them before you drop. Compare row counts before and after to see what you removed. Assign results rather than relying on inplace. Keep the raw file untouched. Date formats like 03/04/2025 are ambiguous, so state the format. Next, summarize the cleaned data.

Check yourself: Why print the row count before and after <code>dropna()</code>?

Answer: To know exactly how many rows you removed and judge whether the loss is acceptable or hides a data problem.

slides.title: Exploratory Analysis in pandas
slides.content:
1. df.describe()
df['Region'].value_counts()
df.groupby('Product')['Sales'].mean()
  2. Use describe() for summary stats.
  3. Use value_counts() for category frequency.
  4. Use groupby() for comparisons.
  5. Spot trends, outliers, and patterns.
  6. EDA helps you understand your data deeply.
    7. Food for the Mind: “Exploration is curiosity in action—ask, group, and discover.”

Worked example: sales by region

Cleaned rows (Region, Sales): Nairobi 500; Meru 300; Nairobi 700; Meru 200; Nakuru 400.

  1. df["Region"].value_counts() gives Nairobi 2, Meru 2, Nakuru 1 (rows per region).
  2. df.groupby("Region")["Sales"].sum() adds sales per region.
  3. Nairobi: 500 + 700 = 1,200. Meru: 300 + 200 = 500. Nakuru: 400.
  4. .sort_values(ascending=False) puts them in order: Nairobi 1200, Meru 500, Nakuru 400.

Check: 1,200 + 500 + 400 = 2,100, and 500 + 300 + 700 + 200 + 400 = 2,100.

Meaning: Nairobi leads. With only two rows each, ask whether the pattern is real before acting.

Concept checkIn a Sales column the mean is KES 5,000 but the median is KES 1,200. What does this most likely suggest?
Practitioner layer

Explore a cleaned sales table.

df.describe()
df["Region"].value_counts()
df.groupby("Product")["Sales"].mean()
df.groupby("Region")["Sales"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
  1. describe() shows count, mean, min and max for numeric columns.
  2. value_counts() shows how many rows per region.
  3. groupby splits by category and applies a sum or mean.
  4. Sorting shows the top region first.

Example reading: if the mean is far above the median, a few very large sales pull it up.

Expert layer

Compare mean and median, and look at min and max for impossible values such as negative quantities. Averages hide variety, so check distribution with a histogram. Use .agg(["sum","mean","count"]) to see several results at once. A pivot in pandas is pd.pivot_table. Always ask whether a pattern is real or just from small groups. Write one finding per question. Next, visualize.

Check yourself: What does <code>df.groupby("Region")["Sales"].sum()</code> return?

Answer: Total sales for each region, as a Series indexed by region.

slides.title: Visualization with matplotlib/seaborn
slides.content:
1. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
sns.barplot(x='Product', y='Sales', data=df)
  2. Use matplotlib for basic charts.
  3. Use seaborn for advanced visuals.
  4. Create bar, line, scatter, and box plots.
  5. Customize titles, labels, and colors.
  6. Save charts as images for reports.
    7. Food for the Mind: “Visuals in Python are your spotlight—shine it where the insight lives.”

Worked example: average versus total bars

Rows (Product, Sales in KES): Sugar 1,200; Sugar 800; Milk 500.

  1. sns.barplot(x="Product", y="Sales", data=df) uses the default average.
  2. Sugar bar: (1,200 + 800) / 2 = 1,000. Milk bar: 500.
  3. Add estimator=sum, errorbar=None.
  4. Sugar bar: 1,200 + 800 = 2,000. Milk bar: 500.
  5. Add title and axis labels with KES units, then plt.savefig("sales_by_product.png", dpi=150) before plt.show().

Meaning: the same data gives a Sugar bar of 1,000 or 2,000 depending on the estimator. Match the chart to the question.

Concept checkYour seaborn bar chart shows the average Sales per product, but your manager wants total Sales per product. What do you change?
Practitioner layer

Chart sales by product.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
sns.barplot(x="Product", y="Sales", data=df, estimator=sum, errorbar=None)
plt.title("Sales by product (KES)")
plt.xlabel("Product")
plt.ylabel("Sales (KES)")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("sales_by_product.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

You should see one bar per product. Call savefig before show, otherwise the file may be blank. By default seaborn plots the average; estimator=sum makes it a total.

Expert layer

Pick the chart for the question: bars to compare, lines for time, scatter for relationships, box plots for spread. Always title, label axes and units. Sort bars for easy reading. Avoid more than a handful of colours. Seaborn argument names change between versions (for instance errorbar), so read the docs for your installed version. Start from clean data; a nice chart of a wrong table is still wrong. Next, practise exporting reports.

Check yourself: Why does your saved PNG sometimes come out blank?

Answer: Calling <code>plt.show()</code> before <code>plt.savefig()</code> can clear the figure. Save first, then show.

slides.title: Automating Data Tasks
slides.content:
1. Use loops to repeat tasks across rows or files.
  2. Use functions to reuse code.
  3. Automate cleaning, analysis, and reporting.
  4. Schedule scripts to run daily or weekly.
  5. Python saves time and reduces errors.
    6. Food for the Mind: “Automation is your time-saver—teach the machine once, and let it run.”

The pandas lessons run in Jupyter on your own computer. This box lets you practise the pure-Python parts right here.

Open the full Playground

Worked example: combine monthly files

The sales folder has 3 monthly files. After clean() they have 120, 135 and 110 rows.

  1. glob.glob("sales/*.csv") lists the three paths.
  2. The loop reads each file and applies clean(), which trims and title-cases names and drops duplicates.
  3. Add print(path, len(df)) inside the loop to log row counts.
  4. pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True) stacks them: 120 + 135 = 255, then 255 + 110 = 365 rows.
  5. to_csv("all_sales.csv", index=False) saves the result.

Meaning: 365 rows should match the logged counts. If it does not, a file went wrong.

Concept checkYour script loops over monthly files, but one file has a differently named column and the loop crashes. What is the best way to make it safer?
Practitioner layer

Clean and summarize every monthly file in a folder.

import pandas as pd, glob

def clean(df):
    df["Name"] = df["Name"].str.strip().str.title()
    return df.drop_duplicates()

frames = []
for path in glob.glob("sales/*.csv"):
    frames.append(clean(pd.read_csv(path)))
all_sales = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
all_sales.to_csv("all_sales.csv", index=False)

The loop reads each file, the function cleans it, and concat stacks the results. Write functions for steps you repeat. To run it daily, schedule the script with Windows Task Scheduler.

Expert layer

Automate only what is stable and checked by hand first. Add print statements or logging so you know what ran and how many rows each file had. Make files consistent: if one has a different column name, the loop will break, so validate columns. Handle errors with try and except and report which file failed. Keep scripts in version control. Do not hard-code private passwords. Next, learn to turn a notebook into a script.

Check yourself: What is the benefit of putting cleaning steps inside a function?

Answer: You write the logic once and reuse it on every file, which prevents inconsistencies and makes changes easier.

slides.title: Exporting Results
slides.content:
1. df.to_csv("cleaned_data.csv", index=False)
  2. Use to_csv() to save cleaned data.
  3. Use to_excel() for Excel output.
  4. Export charts using plt.savefig().
  5. Share results with teams or tools.
  6. Always label and organize your exports.
    7. Food for the Mind: “Exporting is packaging—your insights, ready to deliver.”
Concept checkYou will send a cleaned customer file to a supplier who is not authorised to see customer details. What should you do before sending?
Practitioner layer

Export results for different readers.

df.to_csv("cleaned_data.csv", index=False)
with pd.ExcelWriter("report.xlsx") as w:
    df.to_excel(w, sheet_name="Cleaned", index=False)
    summary.to_excel(w, sheet_name="Summary")
plt.savefig("chart.png", dpi=150)
  1. index=False stops the row numbers being written as a column.
  2. One Excel workbook can hold several sheets.
  3. Name files clearly, for example sales_2025-03_cleaned.csv.

Open the files to confirm they look right. to_excel needs openpyxl installed.

Expert layer

Open every export before sending it. Dates and long IDs can be altered by Excel when it opens a CSV. Use a folder structure like data/raw, data/clean and outputs so nothing is overwritten. Anonymize before sharing: remove names, phone numbers and IDs unless the recipient is authorized. Add a README listing the source and date. Choose the format your reader uses: managers often want Excel or PDF. Next, combine everything into a notebook story.

Check yourself: Why use <code>index=False</code> in <code>to_csv</code>?

Answer: It prevents pandas writing its internal row numbers as an extra unnamed column in the file.

slides.title: Practical: Python Data Project
slides.content:
1. Task:
  2. Choose a dataset and import it using pandas.
  3. Clean the data and perform EDA.
  4. Create at least 2 charts using matplotlib or seaborn.
  5. Export your cleaned data and visuals.
  6. Save your notebook and share your findings.
    7. Food for the Mind: “Your notebook is your narrative—code, clean, and communicate.”

Worked example: monthly sales line

Cleaned rows (Date, Amount in KES): Jan 1,000; Jan 500; Feb 800; Feb 600; Mar 900.

  1. Load with parse_dates=["Date"] so Date is a real date, not text.
  2. Group by month: df.groupby(df["Date"].dt.to_period("M"))["Amount"].sum()
  3. Jan: 1,000 + 500 = 1,500. Feb: 800 + 600 = 1,400. Mar: 900.
  4. Add .plot() for the line chart, then save it as a PNG.

Check: 1,500 + 1,400 + 900 = 3,800, and 1,000 + 500 + 800 + 600 + 900 = 3,800.

Meaning: sales fell from 1,500 to 900 across the three months. Write that finding in a Markdown cell and note any missing months.

Concept checkWhich order fits the Python data project in this lesson?
Practitioner layer

Worked answer with a sales CSV.

  1. Import: df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv", parse_dates=["Date"]); run info().
  2. Clean: strip text, fix Amount with pd.to_numeric, drop_duplicates(), handle blanks, and print row counts.
  3. EDA: describe(), value_counts() on Branch, groupby("Product")["Amount"].sum().
  4. Chart 1: monthly sales line with df.groupby(df["Date"].dt.to_period("M"))["Amount"].sum().plot().
  5. Chart 2: a seaborn bar of sales by branch.
  6. Export cleaned.csv and the PNGs.
  7. Add Markdown cells explaining each finding.

Stretch: write a function that does steps 1-3 for any file.

Expert layer

Write the story as you go: a heading, the question, the code, one sentence of insight. Restart and Run All before sharing to prove it works top to bottom. Remove cells that failed or are no longer needed. Use made-up or public data for a portfolio. Mention limits, such as small samples or missing months. Next, upload the notebook to a public portfolio only after checking no private data is inside.

Check yourself: Why click Restart and Run All before sharing a notebook?

Answer: It proves the notebook works from top to bottom without hidden state from cells run out of order.

slides.title: Q&A
slides.content:
1. What if I get an error? → Read the message and check your syntax.
  2. What if I don’t know Python? → Start with small steps and practice.
  3. What if my chart looks wrong? → Check your data and labels.
  4. What if I forget a command? → Use documentation or search online.
  5. What if I’m stuck? → Ask for help or copy working examples.
    6. Food for the Mind: “Every bug is a lesson—debug, learn, and grow.”

Worked example: fixing a KeyError

The code df["Sales"].sum() stops with an error.

  1. Read the last line first: KeyError: 'Sales'. KeyError means a wrong column name.
  2. Run print(df.columns). It shows Index(['Product', 'Sales ', 'Region']).
  3. Spot the trailing space in 'Sales '.
  4. Fix it: df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()
  5. Run df["Sales"].sum() again. With values 1,200 and 800 it returns 1,200 + 800 = 2,000.

Meaning: read the last line, check the exact names, and change one thing at a time.

Concept checkYour chart looks wrong. What is a sensible first step?
Practitioner layer

Four learner questions:

  • I get an error. Read the last line first: it names the error type. KeyError means a wrong column name; check df.columns.
  • I do not know Python yet. Learn print, variables, lists, loops and functions, then pandas. Twenty minutes a day is enough.
  • My chart looks wrong. Print df.head() and the dtypes, check you are plotting the right columns, and that data was cleaned.
  • I forgot a command. Use help(pd.read_csv) or the official docs.
Expert layer

Debugging is a skill: reproduce the error, shrink the code until it still fails, then read the message. Print intermediate values. Copying working examples is fine, but then change one thing at a time to understand it. If you ask an AI assistant, check what is currently available, paste the error and a tiny made-up sample, never private customer data, and test whatever it suggests yourself. Next, keep a personal snippet file.

Check yourself: You get <code>KeyError: "Sales"</code>. What do you check?

Answer: The exact column names with <code>df.columns</code>. The name may differ in spelling, capitals or have a trailing space.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
slides.content:
1. Python is powerful for data analysis and automation.
  2. Use pandas for importing, cleaning, and exploring data.
  3. Use matplotlib and seaborn for visualization.
  4. Automate tasks and export results efficiently.
  5. You’re now ready to present your analysis.
    6. Food for the Mind: “Python is your analytical engine—fuel it with data, drive it with logic.”

Worked example: a small pipeline run

Raw rows (Region, Sales in KES): Meru 400; Meru 600; Nakuru 500; Nakuru 500 (a duplicate); Kisumu 300.

  1. Import and inspect: 5 rows.
  2. Clean with df.drop_duplicates(): 4 rows remain.
  3. Explore with df.groupby("Region")["Sales"].sum().
  4. Meru: 400 + 600 = 1,000. Nakuru: 500. Kisumu: 300.
  5. Total: 1,000 + 500 + 300 = 1,800.

Without cleaning, Nakuru would show 500 + 500 = 1,000 and the total would be 1,800 + 500 = 2,300.

Meaning: cleaning before charting avoids overstating sales by KES 500. Then chart and export the result.

Concept checkWhich line gives total Sales for each Region, the explore step of the pipeline?
Practitioner layer

Mental model: Python analysis is a pipeline you can rerun. Import, inspect, clean, explore, visualize, export, automate.

Five-minute self-test, without notes:

  1. Write the line that loads a CSV.
  2. Name the three methods to inspect it.
  3. Remove duplicates and trim names.
  4. Get total Sales by Region.
  5. Save a chart and a clean CSV.

If a line is missing, redo it on a small file today. Typing from memory builds the skill faster than rereading.

Expert layer

Fluency comes from small projects done repeatedly. Build a toolkit: a notebook template with your standard import, inspect and clean steps. Always check results against the source. Expert analysts spend most time on questions and data quality, not syntax. Version your work and document assumptions. Next, learn merging tables with pd.merge and then SQL, which pairs naturally with pandas.

Check yourself: Which stage of the pipeline should come before any charting, and why?

Answer: Cleaning, because charts built from untidy data give misleading results.

slides.title: Python Mini-Project
slides.content:
1. Task:
  2. Choose a dataset and complete a mini-project in Python.
  3. Clean the data, perform EDA, and create visuals.
  4. Export your results and write a short summary.
  5. Save your notebook for your portfolio.
  6. Reflect on what you learned.
    7. Food for the Mind: “Your Python project is your proof—show what you’ve built, and how it works.”

Worked example: writing the summary

Totals by product from df.groupby("Product")["Amount"].sum(): Sugar 45,000; Milk 30,000; Rice 25,000 (KES).

  1. Total: 45,000 + 30,000 + 25,000 = 100,000.
  2. Sugar's share: 45,000 / 100,000 = 45%.
  3. Use .nlargest(2) to list the top two: Sugar and Milk.
  4. Write the summary.
  • Finding: Sugar is the top product.
  • Evidence: KES 45,000 out of 100,000, which is 45%.
  • Action: keep sugar well stocked and review why Rice is lowest.

Meaning: numbers support the claim, so a reader can verify it.

Concept checkWhich is the best three-line summary for your mini-project?
Practitioner layer

Worked answer: "Monthly Shop Sales Analysis".

  1. Load sales.csv; check info() and isnull().sum().
  2. Clean: trim text, convert Amount and Date, drop duplicates, document each change.
  3. EDA: total and average by product; top 5 branches with nlargest(5); one question you answer.
  4. Visuals: line of monthly sales; bar of top products.
  5. Export clean_sales.csv and two PNGs.
  6. Write a three-line summary: finding, evidence, suggested action.
  7. Restart and Run All, then save.

Stretch: wrap steps 1-3 into a function and test it on a second month.

Expert layer

Employers and clients like to see reasoning, not only code. Explain why you made each cleaning decision. Test one result by hand in Excel. Keep the notebook tidy with headings and no leftover experiments. Use anonymized or public data. Reflect: what would you improve with more time? Next, redo the same analysis in Power BI or SQL to show you can move between tools.

Check yourself: What should the three-line summary of your mini-project contain?

Answer: The main finding, the evidence supporting it, and a suggested action or next question.

⭐ Activity: Close the lesson. Say each point above out loud in your own words, then give one example from your own life or work. Any point you cannot explain is where to go back and re-read.
Recall round (answer before you look)

Cover the answers. Say or write your answer to each question, then check yourself in the last layer below.

  1. Give one reason a script can beat repeating clicks in Excel each month. (from: Why Python for Data?)
  2. What does <code>df["Sales"].sum()</code> do? (from: Data Structures (lists, dicts, DataFrames))

Check yourself: the answers

Answers, in the same order:

  1. A script repeats the same steps exactly on new data in seconds and leaves a written record of what was done, which reduces errors.
  2. It selects the Sales column and adds up its values.
  3. To know exactly how many rows you removed and judge whether the loss is acceptable or hides a data problem.
  4. Calling <code>plt.show()</code> before <code>plt.savefig()</code> can clear the figure. Save first, then show.
  5. It prevents pandas writing its internal row numbers as an extra unnamed column in the file.
  6. The main finding, the evidence supporting it, and a suggested action or next question.

slides.title: Structuring Your Findings
slides.content:
1. Start with a clear question and summary of your analysis.
  2. Organize insights into themes or categories.
  3. Use bullet points, visuals, and summaries.
  4. Highlight key metrics and trends.
  5. End with recommendations or next steps.
    6. Food for the Mind: Structure turns data into a message—build it like a bridge, strong and clear.
Concept checkYour report on why a salon's profit fell has 12 findings. Which approach best follows good structuring?
Practitioner layer

Build findings like a pyramid: answer on top, proof underneath, detail at the bottom. Write the question and a one-sentence answer first, then group evidence into three themes.

Example: a duka owner asks, "Why did profit fall in March?"

  1. Answer: gross profit fell from KES 182,000 to KES 151,000 because sugar and cooking-oil margins shrank.
  2. Cost theme: a 2 kg sugar pack cost KES 290 in February and KES 315 in March, but the shelf price stayed KES 330.
  3. Volume theme: units sold were flat.
  4. Mix theme: more low-margin items were sold.
  5. Recommendation: raise sugar to KES 350 and re-check weekly.
Expert layer

Weak reports follow the analyst's journey ("first I cleaned, then I tried...") instead of the reader's decision. Senior analysts write the recommendation first, then check that every slide earns its place; anything that does not support the answer moves to an appendix. Keep to about three headline themes, because readers remember very little. Make the themes non-overlapping and together complete (the MECE idea). State the one limitation that could change your answer, such as a small sample or missing weeks. Learn next: the pyramid principle and situation-complication-resolution writing.

Check yourself: You have 14 findings from a clinic waiting-time analysis. How do you decide which go into the main story?

Answer: Keep only findings that directly support the answer to your stated question, grouped into about three non-overlapping themes. Move the rest to an appendix so the reader is not forced to sort them.

slides.title: Building a Compelling Story
slides.content:
1. Use the “Data → Insight → Action” flow.
  2. Introduce the problem, show the evidence, and suggest solutions.
  3. Keep it simple, logical, and engaging.
  4. Use real-world examples to connect with your audience.
  5. Every chart should support your story.
    6. Food for the Mind: Data storytelling is persuasion with proof—make your case with clarity.
Concept checkA sacco chart is titled 'Takings by day'. Which rewrite best follows Data, Insight, Action?
Practitioner layer

Data → Insight → Action means every chart ends with a "so what". Data is the fact, insight is its meaning, action is what someone does on Monday. Write all three as sentences before you draw anything.

Example for a matatu sacco: Data: Route 46 earns about KES 3,100 per vehicle on weekdays but KES 1,900 on Sundays. Insight: the Sunday gap comes from empty afternoon return trips. Action: move two vehicles to the Sunday market route for four Sundays and compare takings.

Then choose the chart: columns of daily takings per vehicle, Sunday highlighted in one colour, with the title "Sunday takings are 39% lower on Route 46". Check: (3,100 - 1,900) / 3,100 = 0.387.

Expert layer

Stories persuade partly by what they leave out, but never leave out what would change the conclusion. Test yours with the sceptic's question: what would make this wrong? Name the strongest alternative explanation (rain, school holidays, a road closure) and show you checked it. Beware the narrative fallacy: a smooth story built after the fact can fit pure noise. Separate correlation from cause, and say how confident you are. Learn next: action titles, the situation-complication-resolution structure, and running small pilots so your recommendation can be tested.

Check yourself: A chart is titled 'Sales by month'. Rewrite the title as an insight and say what changes for the reader.

Answer: For example: 'Sales dip every February, so order less stock in January.' The reader gets the conclusion and the action immediately instead of having to decode the chart themselves.

slides.title: Creating Effective Slides
slides.content:
1. Use clean layouts with minimal text.
  2. Highlight one insight per slide.
  3. Use visuals instead of tables when possible.
  4. Choose readable fonts and consistent colors.
  5. Practice slide flow and transitions.
    6. Food for the Mind: Slides are your stage—design them to spotlight your message.
Concept checkA boutique slide shows return rates for 12 categories in a table, and dresses stand out. What should you do?
Practitioner layer

One slide, one message. Write the message as a full-sentence title, then keep only the visual that proves it.

Example: a boutique reviewing returns. Title: "Dresses are returned far more often than any other category". Steps:

  1. Compute return rate per category: returned units / units sold.
  2. Use a sorted horizontal bar chart, one accent colour for dresses, grey for the rest.
  3. Delete gridlines and the legend; label bars directly.
  4. Use at least 18 pt text so the back row can read it.
  5. Put the detailed table in the appendix or speaker notes.

Test: cover the title; if the chart no longer says the point, add labels or an annotation.

Expert layer

Slides are for the room; documents are for reading later. Do not use one deck for both or it becomes crowded and serves neither. Check accessibility: sufficient contrast, never red versus green alone, readable on a phone and on a weak projector, where colours and small text often fail. Use a slide master so titles, fonts and colours stay aligned across slides. Keep a backup appendix of tables and extra charts for questions. Learn next: action titles, decluttering charts, and building a reusable PowerPoint template.

Check yourself: Your slide shows a 40-row table of branch sales. What do you do?

Answer: Decide the one insight (for example, which three branches lag), show only that in a sorted, highlighted bar chart, and move the full table to the appendix or a handout.

slides.title: Presenting with Confidence
slides.content:
1. Know your content—practice until it feels natural.
  2. Speak clearly and make eye contact.
  3. Use pauses to emphasize key points.
  4. Handle nerves with deep breaths and preparation.
  5. Confidence comes from clarity and practice.
    6. Food for the Mind: Confidence isn’t loud—it’s clear, calm, and ready.
Concept checkYour 10-minute talk has 5 slides and ran 14 minutes in rehearsal. What is the best fix?
Practitioner layer

Confidence is preparation you can measure. Use a four-step rehearsal:

  1. Write the first sentence you will say for each slide.
  2. Rehearse aloud with a timer, three times.
  3. Mark a pause after each key number.
  4. Record yourself once on your phone and watch it.

Example: for a 10-minute slot with 5 slides, plan about 1.5 minutes per slide and keep 2 minutes for questions. Say "Takings rose to KES 412,000", pause two seconds, then explain. Open with your answer, not an apology. If you lose your place, look at the slide, breathe, restate its title, and continue. Arrive early to test the screen and clicker.

Expert layer

Nerves are normal and usually less visible than you think. Rehearse your opening and closing most, since they are where you feel most exposed. Plan for failure: keep a PDF on your phone and a one-page printed summary in case the laptop or projector dies. Do not read the slides; slides hold the evidence and you hold the explanation. Record yourself to spot filler words and rushing. After each talk, ask a trusted colleague for one thing to keep and one to change. Learn next: structured openings and handling a hostile room.

Check yourself: Your 10-minute talk with 5 slides ran 14 minutes in rehearsal. What do you cut first, and why not just speak faster?

Answer: Cut material that does not support your single answer, usually method detail and secondary charts, and move it to the appendix. Speaking faster removes the pauses that let key numbers land and makes you look nervous.

slides.title: Data-Driven Decision Making
slides.content:
1. Use insights to support business or policy decisions.
  2. Show how your findings solve real problems.
  3. Link data to goals, KPIs, or outcomes.
  4. Use “if-then” logic to guide action.
  5. Decision-makers want clarity, not complexity.
    6. Food for the Mind: Data is your compass—use it to guide smart decisions.
Concept checkYour analysis shows Branch A sells more than Branch B. The owner asks if B should close. What is the best response?
Practitioner layer

A decision needs three things: the options, the metric that judges them, and a threshold. Then write it as if-then logic: "If X, do Y; otherwise Z."

Example: a dukakeeper wonders whether to open until 10 pm. Record two weeks of takings between 8 and 10 pm (cash plus M-Pesa): the average is KES 1,400 a night. At a 25% gross margin, that is KES 350 of gross profit. The extra cost (electricity and an attendant) is KES 900 a night.

Rule: "If evening gross profit exceeds extra cost, open late." 350 is less than 900, so do not open late; revisit if evening takings reach about KES 3,600 (900 / 0.25).

Expert layer

Decisions fail more from the wrong question than from missing data. Agree the decision, its owner and its deadline before you start; analysis nobody will act on is waste. Show uncertainty as ranges or scenarios (worst, expected, best), and say what result would change your recommendation. Watch for proxy traps, such as optimising footfall or clicks when the goal is profit. Record decisions and revisit outcomes later; that loop is how you learn what your analysis was worth. Learn next: decision trees, expected value, and pilot or A/B testing.

Check yourself: Your analysis shows Branch A sells more than Branch B. Is that enough to recommend closing B?

Answer: No. Sales alone ignore costs, trends and context. You need profit, the cost and consequences of closing, and whether B is improving, all tied to the goal metric the owner cares about.

slides.title: Executive Summaries
slides.content:
1. Summarize your findings in one page or slide.
  2. Include the question, key insights, and recommendations.
  3. Use bullet points and visuals for quick reading.
  4. Tailor language for non-technical audiences.
  5. Executive summaries help leaders act fast.
    6. Food for the Mind: Executives don’t need the whole story—just the headline and the punchline.

Worked example: A clinic executive summary

A clinic manager asks why Monday waits are so long. Build the summary from the numbers.

  1. Compare arrivals: 96 on Mondays versus 70 on other days.
  2. Find the gap: 96 - 70 = 26 more arrivals.
  3. Convert to a percentage: 26 / 70 = 0.371, about 37% more.
  4. Compare waits: median 74 minutes versus 41, so 74 - 41 = 33 minutes longer.

Summary page: Question: why are Monday waits long? Answer: Monday has about 37% more arrivals with the same staff. Recommendation: move one nurse from Thursday to Monday mornings for four weeks and track the median wait.

What it means: every number has a comparison, so a reader who sees only this page can act.

Concept checkWhich opening best suits an executive summary for a hospital manager?
Practitioner layer

Write the summary last, but place it first. Use four blocks: Question, Answer, Evidence (three bullets with numbers), Recommendation with owner and date. Keep it to one page.

Example for a clinic:

  • Question: why are Monday waits so long?
  • Answer: Monday has about 37% more arrivals with the same staff.
  • Evidence: 96 arrivals on Mondays versus 70 on other days; median wait 74 minutes versus 41; only one clinical officer on triage before 10 am.
  • Recommendation: the manager moves one nurse from Thursday to Monday mornings for four weeks and tracks median wait.

Test: a reader who reads only this page can act.

Expert layer

Executives skim the first lines and the numbers. Put the decision needed in the first sentence ("Approve X by Y"). Every number needs a comparison (last month, target, other branch) or it means little. Do not bury caveats; one honest line on the biggest limitation builds trust. Keep figures identical across summary, slides and appendix by pulling them from one source cell or query, because one mismatch destroys credibility. Learn next: bottom-line-up-front writing and one-page decision memos.

Check yourself: A draft summary begins 'In this report we cleaned the data and ran several analyses...'. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

Answer: It describes your process instead of what the reader needs. Start with the answer and the decision requested, then the evidence, then the recommendation.

slides.title: Presenting to Non-Technical Audiences
slides.content:
1. Avoid jargon—use plain language.
  2. Focus on impact, not process.
  3. Use analogies or examples to explain concepts.
  4. Highlight what matters to the audience.
  5. Keep visuals simple and intuitive.
    6. Food for the Mind: Speak human, not machine—make your insights relatable.
Concept checkYou tell a shop owner 'the data shows high variance in daily till revenue'. How should you restate it?
Practitioner layer

Translate three things: terms, numbers and methods. Replace "churn" with "customers who stopped buying". Convert statistics into what people can feel. Describe your method in one sentence; keep the rest for the appendix.

Example: instead of "high variance in daily till revenue", say: "Daily takings jump around a lot, from KES 8,000 one day to KES 20,000 the next, so ordering stock based on one day is risky."

For a correlation of 0.7: "When A goes up, B usually goes up too, but that does not prove A causes B." End every point with "what this means for you". Use one analogy per idea, such as a forecast range like a weather forecast.
