Expert layer

Simplifying is not dumbing down; you must understand an idea deeply to explain it simply. Avoid analogies that mislead, such as "the model learns like a child". Know the audience: a clinic matron cares about patient safety, a finance officer about cash. Pre-wire important meetings by sharing the summary with a key stakeholder beforehand so there are no surprises. Check understanding by asking someone to explain your point back. Learn next: audience mapping and plain-language writing.

Check yourself: How would you explain to a shop owner that the 95% confidence interval for average monthly profit is KES 40,000 to 48,000?

Answer: Say: 'From the months we looked at, we are fairly sure your typical monthly profit is between KES 40,000 and 48,000. We cannot give one exact number because we only saw part of the picture.'

slides.title: Handling Questions
slides.content:
1. Listen fully before answering.
  2. Repeat the question to clarify.
  3. Use data to support your response.
  4. Admit when you don’t know—offer to follow up.
  5. Stay calm and respectful.
    6. Food for the Mind: Questions aren’t attacks—they’re invitations to explain.
Concept checkA manager says your sales figure is wrong and you have not verified everything. What do you do?
Practitioner layer

Use a four-step response: Listen, Restate, Answer, Check. Restate: "You are asking whether the dip is only in Kisumu?" Answer with the number first, one line of why, then point to the evidence slide. Check: "Does that answer it?" For unknowns: "I have not split it by age group. I will check and send it by Thursday", then actually send it.

Example: "Is your sample big enough?" Answer: "We have 412 receipts across three weeks. For the overall trend that is adequate; for single products it is thin, so treat product-level figures as indicative."

Before presenting, list the five hardest questions and prepare backup slides.

Expert layer

Never guess: one invented answer damages trust in everything else. Distinguish "I do not know" from "the data cannot say". If someone finds a real error, thank them, fix it and send corrected figures within a day. Separate question types: clarification, challenge, and politics (someone fighting a decision); take politics offline. Keep a Q&A log after each presentation, because repeated questions show where your analysis or story is weak. Learn next: stakeholder analysis and basic negotiation.

Check yourself: A manager says 'Your numbers must be wrong, I know sales are up', and you have not verified everything. How do you respond?

Answer: Stay calm, restate the claim, show how your figure was calculated and from what source, and offer to reconcile it with theirs (different period or definition is common). Do not argue, and do not concede before checking.

slides.title: Portfolio Building
slides.content:
1. Save your best projects and presentations.
  2. Include visuals, summaries, and code (if applicable).
  3. Use GitHub, LinkedIn, or a personal website.
  4. Update regularly with new work.
  5. Your portfolio is your professional showcase.
    6. Food for the Mind: Your portfolio is your passport—stamp it with every skill you earn.
Concept checkA hiring manager sees a portfolio with ten notebooks and no write-ups. Why is it weaker than three explained case studies?
Practitioner layer

A portfolio is three to five projects, each written as a short case study: Problem, Data (source, size, limits), Method, Result, Next steps, plus a link to the workbook or code.

Example GitHub layout for "duka-sales-analysis":

README.md      question, finding, one chart
data/          small public or synthetic sample
queries/       SQL or notebooks
outputs/       charts and slide PDF

Steps: pick the project; write a 150-word summary at the top of the README; add your best chart; include dependencies so it runs; link it from LinkedIn. Never upload private client data; anonymise or use public or synthetic data. A stranger should understand it in two minutes.

Expert layer

Quality beats quantity: reviewers skim, so the first screen must show the question and the finding. Show range with different kinds of work, for example a dashboard, a SQL project, a Python analysis and a presentation. Respect confidentiality: client or employer data needs permission and anonymising. Keep repositories tidy, and never commit passwords or keys. Write about decisions you made and mistakes you corrected, because that shows judgement. Learn next: README writing, Git basics, and a simple personal page for your best work.

Check yourself: Why might ten unexplained notebooks be weaker than three well-explained projects?

Answer: Reviewers cannot see your thinking or the result in unexplained notebooks. A case study with question, method, finding and limitations shows judgement and communication, which employers and clients value most.

slides.title: Practical: Present Your Analysis
slides.content:
1. Task:
  2. Choose a completed project from a previous module.
  3. Create a 5-slide presentation with visuals and insights.
  4. Include an executive summary and recommendations.
  5. Present to a peer or mentor and get feedback.
  6. Save your slides for your portfolio.
    7. Food for the Mind: Your presentation is your spotlight—step up and shine.
Concept checkAfter you present, your peer cannot say what your recommendation was. What is the best conclusion?
Practitioner layer
  1. Pick a finished project, for example the duka sales workbook. Write the question and the answer in one sentence each.
  2. Pull the three numbers that prove the answer.
  3. Build 5 slides: (1) executive summary, (2) finding 1 chart, (3) finding 2 chart, (4) limitations and method in three bullets, (5) recommendations and next steps.
  4. Write sentence titles that state each insight.
  5. Rehearse aloud twice with a 5-minute timer.
  6. Present to a peer; ask them to write the one thing they remember and the one confusing point.
  7. Revise and save as PDF for your portfolio.

Expected result: your peer repeats your answer in one sentence. Stretch: present again in 3 minutes to someone outside data.

Expert layer

Common failures: default charts pasted in, five findings on one slide, and no recommendation. Use the one-sentence test: if the peer cannot repeat your conclusion, the deck failed, not the peer. Keep versions (v1, v2) and note which feedback you applied; that history is strong portfolio evidence. Time yourself, because first drafts almost always run long. Senior analysts rehearse with someone who will interrupt. Learn next: slide masters and templates, and presenting live from a dashboard without getting lost.

Check yourself: After you present, your peer cannot say what your recommendation was. Whose problem is that?

Answer: Yours, not the peer's. The recommendation was probably buried or vague. Put it on the summary slide and the final slide as one plain sentence with an owner and a date.

slides.title: Q&A
slides.content:
1. What if I’m nervous? → Practice and breathe—confidence grows with repetition.
  2. What if I get a tough question? → Stay calm, clarify, and respond with logic.
  3. What if my slides are too long? → Trim to essentials—less is more.
  4. What if I forget something? → Keep notes or cue cards.
  5. What if I’m presenting online? → Test your tech and engage visually.
    6. Food for the Mind: Every presenter starts unsure—practice turns nerves into power.

Worked example: Trimming a 10-minute talk

You have 10 minutes and a first draft of 12 slides.

  1. Apply the ceiling of about one slide per minute: 10 minutes gives at most 10 slides.
  2. Aim lower, at 5 to 7 slides. Choose 6.
  3. Check the pace: 10 minutes / 6 slides = 1.67 minutes, about 1 minute 40 seconds per slide, which leaves room for pauses after key numbers.
  4. Count what moves: 12 - 6 = 6 slides go to the appendix.
  5. Add a one-line prompt in your notes for each of the 6 slides in case you lose your place.

Result: 6 main slides and 6 backup slides. Meaning: the audience gets the answer without rushing, and the appendix is ready if someone asks a tough question.

Concept checkSomeone asks a question mid-slide that you will cover two slides later. What is the best handling?
Practitioner layer

"I freeze on tough questions. What do I do?" Pause two seconds, restate the question, answer in one sentence with a number, then stop talking. If you do not know, give a date for follow-up.

"How many slides is too many?" Treat about one slide per minute as a ceiling, not a target. For 10 minutes, aim for 5 to 7 and keep the rest in an appendix.

"How do I keep people engaged online?" Ask a direct question every few minutes, use chat or polls, share one screen, send the PDF beforehand for weak connections.

"What if I forget my words?" Put one prompt line per slide in your notes; if lost, read the slide title and continue.

Expert layer

Under most nerves is the fear of being exposed as not knowing. Make "I do not know yet; here is how I will find out" a normal professional sentence. Record yourself monthly so progress becomes visible. For online sessions, bandwidth varies: avoid video and heavy animation, and have a fallback plan. Seek low-stakes repetition, such as a meetup lightning talk or a short team briefing. Ask for structured feedback: one thing that worked, one to change. Learn next: storytelling basics and facilitation.

Check yourself: Someone asks a question mid-slide that you will cover two slides later. How do you handle it?

Answer: Acknowledge it, say it is covered shortly and name where, then answer it properly when you arrive. If it is essential to understanding the current slide, give a brief answer now.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
slides.content:
1. Structure your findings into a clear, compelling story.
  2. Use visuals and summaries to communicate effectively.
  3. Present with confidence and clarity.
  4. Tailor your message to your audience.
  5. Your analysis deserves to be seen and understood.
    6. Food for the Mind: Insight is only powerful when it’s shared—present like it matters.
Concept checkYour chart is correct but nobody acted on it. Which is the most likely communication cause?
Practitioner layer

Mental model: Question, Answer, Evidence, Action, shaped for a specific audience. Structure is the skeleton (pyramid), story is the flow (Data, Insight, Action), slides are the visual proof (one message each), delivery is clarity under pressure, and the executive summary is the front door. Everything bends to the reader's decision.

Five-minute self-test, on paper:

  1. Write your project's answer in one sentence.
  2. Rewrite one chart title as an insight.
  3. Name the one number a manager should remember.
  4. Write the recommendation with an owner and a date.
  5. List the hardest question you expect and your answer.

Any item that takes over a minute shows what to fix.

Expert layer

One analysis often needs three deliverables: a one-page memo, a five-minute talk, and a full appendix. Senior analysts choose the format from the audience and the decision, not from habit. Keep a reusable template (summary page, slide master, chart style) so your time goes into thinking, not formatting. Always ask what you want people to do or decide afterwards. Judge your communication by results: was the decision made, was the recommendation adopted, were the questions answered? Learn next: stakeholder management and dashboard storytelling.

Check yourself: Your chart is correct but nobody acted on it. Name two likely communication causes.

Answer: The takeaway was never stated (no insight title or recommendation), and the message was not tailored to the audience's decision, for example too much jargon or too many competing points.

slides.title: Presentation Task
slides.content:
1. Task:
  2. Choose a dataset and complete a full analysis.
  3. Create a 5-slide presentation with visuals, insights, and recommendations.
  4. Include an executive summary and prepare to present.
  5. Record or deliver your presentation to a peer.
  6. Reflect on what you learned and improve your slides.
    7. Food for the Mind: Your challenge is to speak insight—make your data heard.
Concept checkYour slide total says KES 1,840,000 but the pivot table says KES 1,790,000. What do you do before presenting?
Practitioner layer
  1. Choose a dataset and write the question, such as "Which products earn the most profit at my duka?"
  2. Clean it: remove duplicates, fix dates, check units. Write each rule in a cleaning log.
  3. Analyse, for example df.groupby("product")["profit"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False).
  4. Pick two charts that answer the question.
  5. Build 5 slides: summary, finding 1, finding 2, caveats, recommendation.
  6. Record 5 minutes on your phone or present to a peer.
  7. Write a 150-word reflection, change two things, record again.

Expected result: a 5-slide deck, a cleaning log, a recording and a revised version. Stretch: make a one-page summary for a non-technical reader.

Expert layer

Most of a full analysis is invisible work: cleaning decisions, definitions and checks. Make it reproducible so that when a manager asks "why 4,213?" you can show the steps. Reconcile: totals on slides must equal totals in the data. State assumptions explicitly. Watch for duplicates inflating totals, missing periods and survivorship. The recording is a gift: you will hear filler words and notice slides you read aloud. Learn next: writing a short methodology note and version-controlling your work.

Check yourself: Your slide total says KES 1,840,000 but your pivot says KES 1,790,000. What do you do before presenting?

Answer: Stop and reconcile: find the KES 50,000 gap (filters, duplicates, date range, copy-paste error), fix the source, and make every figure come from one calculation. Never present numbers that disagree.

slides.title: Lock It In: Module Recap
slides.content:
1. Structuring Your Findings: Start with a clear question and summary of your analysis.
  2. Building a Compelling Story: Use the “Data → Insight → Action” flow.
  3. Presenting with Confidence: Know your content—practice until it feels natural.
  4. Data-Driven Decision Making: Use insights to support business or policy decisions.
  5. Presenting to Non-Technical Audiences: Avoid jargon—use plain language.
  6. Handling Questions: Listen fully before answering.
  7. Practical: Present Your Analysis: Choose a completed project from a previous module.
  8. Presentation Task: Choose a dataset and complete a full analysis.
⭐ Activity: Close the lesson. Say each point above out loud in your own words, then give one example from your own life or work. Any point you cannot explain is where to go back and re-read.
Recall round (answer before you look)

Cover the answers. Say or write your answer to each question, then check yourself in the last layer below.

  1. You have 14 findings from a clinic waiting-time analysis. How do you decide which go into the main story? (from: Structuring Your Findings)
  2. Your slide shows a 40-row table of branch sales. What do you do? (from: Creating Effective Slides)
  3. Your analysis shows Branch A sells more than Branch B. Is that enough to recommend closing B? (from: Data-Driven Decision Making)
  4. How would you explain to a shop owner that the 95% confidence interval for average monthly profit is KES 40,000 to 48,000? (from: Presenting to Non-Technical Audiences)
  5. Why might ten unexplained notebooks be weaker than three well-explained projects? (from: Portfolio Building)
  6. Your slide total says KES 1,840,000 but your pivot says KES 1,790,000. What do you do before presenting? (from: Presentation Task)
Teach it back
  1. Explain the three ideas you find hardest to a friend or family member in two minutes, without notes.
  2. Wherever you stumble, write the lesson name down and go back to it. Re-read the Practice layer and redo the activity.
  3. This week, use one idea from this module in real life or work, and note what happened.
  4. Come back in two days and answer the recall questions again. Remembering after a gap is what makes it stay.

Lessons to revisit if needed:

  • Structuring Your Findings
  • Building a Compelling Story
  • Presenting with Confidence
  • Data-Driven Decision Making
  • Presenting to Non-Technical Audiences
  • Handling Questions
  • Practical: Present Your Analysis
  • Presentation Task
Check yourself: the answers

Answers, in the same order:

  1. Keep only findings that directly support the answer to your stated question, grouped into about three non-overlapping themes. Move the rest to an appendix so the reader is not forced to sort them.
  2. Decide the one insight (for example, which three branches lag), show only that in a sorted, highlighted bar chart, and move the full table to the appendix or a handout.
  3. No. Sales alone ignore costs, trends and context. You need profit, the cost and consequences of closing, and whether B is improving, all tied to the goal metric the owner cares about.
  4. Say: 'From the months we looked at, we are fairly sure your typical monthly profit is between KES 40,000 and 48,000. We cannot give one exact number because we only saw part of the picture.'
  5. Reviewers cannot see your thinking or the result in unexplained notebooks. A case study with question, method, finding and limitations shows judgement and communication, which employers and clients value most.
  6. Stop and reconcile: find the KES 50,000 gap (filters, duplicates, date range, copy-paste error), fix the source, and make every figure come from one calculation. Never present numbers that disagree.

slides.title: What is AI in Data Analytics?
slides.content:
1. AI refers to machines that mimic human intelligence—learning, reasoning, and decision-making.
  2. In data analytics, AI helps automate tasks and uncover patterns.
  3. It includes machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision.
  4. AI can analyze large datasets faster than humans.
  5. It’s transforming industries and workflows.
    6. Food for the Mind: AI doesn’t replace analysts—it empowers them to think bigger and faster.
Concept checkA boutique owner has 2,000 customer comments and wants them grouped into themes like delivery, price and sizes. Which branch of AI fits?
Practitioner layer

Think of AI in analytics as three jobs: machine learning finds patterns in numbers, NLP reads text, computer vision reads images. Example: a shop owner has 2,000 customer comments about a boutique. An NLP tool can group them into themes such as "delivery late", "price" and "sizes". Then you count each theme.

  1. Export comments with no names or phone numbers.
  2. Ask the tool to tag each comment with one theme.
  3. Read 30 tags yourself.
  4. Count with a PivotTable: 400 "delivery" out of 2,000 = 20%.

The AI saved reading time. You still decided what the themes mean for the business.

Expert layer

AI is fast, not automatically right. Its output is a draft until you test it. Pro habit: always sample-check, say 20 to 30 rows, before trusting a whole result. Edge case: AI can sound confident while inventing a number or a column that does not exist. Expert thinking: ask "what would I expect to see if this were correct?" and compare. Learn next: basic statistics, because you cannot judge a model you cannot sanity-check.

Check yourself: Name the three branches of AI mentioned on this slide and give one analytics task for each.

Answer: Machine learning (predicting sales from past sales), natural language processing (grouping customer comments into themes), computer vision (reading text or counting items from photos of receipts or shelves).

slides.title: AI Tools for Analysts
slides.content:
1. ChatGPT helps generate summaries, explanations, and code.
  2. Microsoft Copilot assists with Excel, Power BI, and presentations.
  3. AI tools can clean data, suggest visuals, and write queries.
  4. They save time and reduce manual effort.
  5. Analysts must guide AI with clear instructions.
    6. Food for the Mind: AI is your assistant—not your replacement. Use it wisely, lead it boldly.

Worked example: Test an AI-written formula

You asked a tool for revenue per item and got =SUMPRODUCT((B2:B6="Sugar")*C2:C6*D2:D6). Test it on five dummy rows (Item in B, Qty in C, Price_KES in D).

  1. Row 2: Sugar, 3, 330
  2. Row 3: Maize flour, 2, 150
  3. Row 4: Sugar, 2, 330
  4. Row 5: Sugar, 1, 330
  5. Row 6: Cooking oil, 1, 250

Work it out by hand, using only the Sugar rows: (3 x 330) + (2 x 330) + (1 x 330) = 990 + 660 + 330 = 1,980.

Enter the formula. Excel returns 1,980, which matches.

Meaning: the formula is correct on a table where you know the answer, so it can be trusted on the real sheet. No customer data was shared.

Concept checkYou want an AI tool to write a revenue-per-item formula for your duka. What should you paste into a public chatbot?
Practitioner layer

A good prompt has four parts: role, context, task, format. Weak: "analyse my sales". Strong:

You are a data analyst helping a duka owner.
My table has columns: Date, Item, Qty, Price_KES.
Task: write an Excel formula for total revenue per item.
Format: give the formula, then explain it in 2 lines.

Expected answer is something like =SUMPRODUCT((B2:B500="Sugar")*C2:C500*D2:D500). Never paste real customer names, phone numbers or M-Pesa statements into a public tool. Paste only 5 dummy rows with the same column names. Then test the formula on a few rows you can add by hand.

Expert layer

Different tools suit different jobs, and what is available changes often, so check what your employer or school allows and what is currently on offer. Pro habit: ask the tool to explain every formula, then test it on a tiny table where you know the answer. If the result is wrong, paste the error message back and ask for a fix. Keep a personal prompt notebook of prompts that worked. Learn next: Power Query, so AI-written steps are repeatable.

Check yourself: Why should you give the AI your column names but not your real customer rows?

Answer: The column names are enough for it to write correct formulas or queries, while real rows may contain private data such as names, phone numbers or M-Pesa details that should not go into a public tool. Test the result on dummy rows instead.

slides.title: Automating Data Cleaning with AI
slides.content:
1. AI can detect missing values, duplicates, and outliers.
  2. Tools like OpenRefine and Python libraries use AI to clean data.
  3. AI learns patterns and applies fixes across datasets.
  4. Reduces human error and speeds up preparation.
  5. Analysts still need to review and validate results.
    6. Food for the Mind: Let AI sweep the floor—but you decide what stays and what goes.

Worked example: Check an AI cleaning plan

A clinic sheet has 120 visit rows. AI suggested this code:

df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["visit_id"])
bad = df[(df["age"] < 0) | (df["age"] > 110)]
print(len(df), len(bad))

  1. Keep the raw file untouched and note rows before: 120.
  2. Run the code. It prints 112 3.
  3. Rows removed as duplicates: 120 - 112 = 8. Open them and confirm they are true repeats.
  4. Read the 3 flagged rows: ages 250, 130 and -1. Ask the clinic whether 250 is a typo for 25.

Log: rows before 120, after 112, 8 duplicates removed, 3 ages queried. Meaning: AI found the problems, but you decided what to fix.

Concept checkAn AI cleaning tool deletes 300 rows it called outliers. What should you do first?
Practitioner layer

Say a clinic sheet has patient ages with a stray 250 and duplicate visit rows. Ask AI for a cleaning plan first, not a cleaned file. In pandas it may suggest:

df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["visit_id"])
df["age"] = pd.to_numeric(df["age"], errors="coerce")
bad = df[(df["age"] < 0) | (df["age"] > 110)]
print(len(df), len(bad))

Run it, then read the bad rows yourself. Is 250 a typo for 25, or an unknown? Only someone who knows the clinic can say. Write each decision in a cleaning log: rows before, rows after, what changed and why.

Expert layer

Silent damage is the danger. An automatic fix may fill missing values with an average, merge two different people into one, or delete a real but unusual value. Always keep the raw file untouched and compare row counts before and after. An outlier is a question, not an error: a KES 500,000 sale may be a real bulk order. Fixing the same problem the same way every time matters, so save the steps as a script or Power Query. Learn next: data validation rules.

Check yourself: An AI tool deletes 300 rows it called outliers. What do you check before accepting this?

Answer: Look at the deleted rows to see whether they are errors or real unusual cases, compare row counts and totals before and after, and keep the raw file. Record your decision in a cleaning log.

slides.title: AI for Data Visualization
slides.content:
1. AI can suggest the best chart for your data.
  2. Tools like Power BI and Tableau use AI to auto-generate visuals.
  3. AI can detect trends and highlight insights.
  4. Some platforms offer natural language queries for visuals.
  5. Helps non-technical users explore data easily.
    6. Food for the Mind: AI turns data into pictures—fast, smart, and surprisingly beautiful.
Concept checkAn AI tool suggests a pie chart with 12 slices for monthly M-Pesa takings. What is the best fix?
Practitioner layer

Chart choice follows the question. Compare categories: bar chart. Change over time: line chart. Share of a whole with 2 to 4 parts: simple bar or pie. Two numbers: scatter plot. Example: monthly M-Pesa takings for a shop, Jan to Dec, is a line.

  1. In Power BI, select the Month and Takings fields.
  2. Look at which visual it picks.
  3. Ask yourself: does it answer my question?
  4. Change the visual type if not, and add a title that states the finding, such as "Takings dip in February".

With Copilot or Q&A, type "takings by month", but still check the axis starts at zero for bars.

Expert layer

Auto-generated visuals can be misleading: truncated axes, too many colours, a pie with ten slices, or a pattern that is just noise. Pro habit: write the question first, then judge the chart by whether the reader gets the answer in five seconds. Be careful with "insights" such as automatic trend highlights. They find patterns, not causes. Check the sample size behind each one. Learn next: chart design basics, labelling and colour use.

Check yourself: A tool suggests a pie chart with 12 slices for monthly sales. What would you change and why?

Answer: Use a line chart for change over time, or a bar chart if comparing months. Twelve slices are hard to compare, and the question is about months, not parts of a whole.

slides.title: Predictive Analytics Basics
slides.content:
1. Predictive analytics uses historical data to forecast future outcomes.
  2. AI models learn patterns and make predictions.
  3. Common techniques: regression, classification, clustering.
  4. Used in finance, health, marketing, and logistics.
  5. Requires clean data and careful model selection.
    6. Food for the Mind: Prediction isn’t magic—it’s math, memory, and machine learning.
Concept checkA microfinance team wants to predict whether each customer will repay or default. Which technique fits?
Practitioner layer

Simplest prediction: linear regression. Suppose a duka tracks weekly ad spend (KES) and sales (KES):

SpendSales
1,00020,000
2,00026,000
3,00034,000

In Excel: =FORECAST.LINEAR(4000, B2:B4, A2:A4) gives the sales expected at KES 4,000 spend, about 40,000 on this line. In Python, scikit-learn does the same with LinearRegression().fit(X, y). Steps: clean data, split into training and test rows, fit, check errors on the test rows, only then predict.

Expert layer

Three questions beat any fancy model: is the data clean, does the past resemble the future, and how wrong is it usually? Common traps: using too little data, testing on the same rows you trained on, and mistaking correlation for cause. Three points above are for learning only. Regression predicts a number, classification a category (will this customer repay?), clustering finds groups without labels. Always report a likely range, not one exact figure. Learn next: train/test splits and error measures.

Check yourself: What is the difference between regression and classification, with one example of each?

Answer: Regression predicts a number, such as next month's sales in KES. Classification predicts a category, such as whether a loan will be repaid or defaulted.

slides.title: Ethics in AI & Data
slides.content:
1. AI must be fair, transparent, and accountable.
  2. Bias in data leads to unfair outcomes.
  3. Analysts must check for discrimination and misuse.
  4. Privacy and consent are critical.
  5. Ethical AI builds trust and protects people.
    6. Food for the Mind: Smart analysis is ethical analysis—data without conscience is dangerous.
Concept checkA loan model approves 70 of 100 men but 40 of 100 women. A colleague says to delete the gender column and move on. Your view?
Practitioner layer

Ethics becomes practical through a short checklist you run on every project:

  1. Consent: was the data collected for this use?
  2. Minimise: remove names, IDs, phone numbers you do not need.
  3. Bias test: compare results by group. Example: a loan model approves 70 of 100 men's applications but 40 of 100 women's. Ask why before using it.
  4. Explain: can you tell a person why they were scored this way?
  5. Review: who is accountable if it is wrong?

Write the answers in one page and attach them to the report.

Expert layer

Bias often hides in the data, not the algorithm. If past decisions were unfair, a model trained on them copies the unfairness. Removing an obvious column such as gender does not always help, because other fields like location can act as a stand-in. Pro habit: involve the people affected, and keep a human able to override. In Kenya, the Data Protection Act applies to personal data, so ask your organisation what rules govern your project. Learn next: data protection basics and fairness testing.

Check yourself: A model's approval rate differs sharply between two groups. Name two steps you take before using it.

Answer: Investigate the cause, for example by checking whether the training data reflects past unfair decisions or whether another column acts as a stand-in. Then fix or drop the model, and keep a human reviewer able to override.

slides.title: AI in Excel, Power BI, Python
slides.content:
1. Excel: Copilot suggests formulas and summaries.
  2. Power BI: AI visuals and natural language queries.
  3. Python: AI libraries like scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and transformers.
  4. AI enhances each tool’s capabilities.
  5. Learn to integrate AI into your workflow.
    6. Food for the Mind: AI is the upgrade—your tools just got smarter.

Worked example: One task, three tools

Task: total sales by region from five rows: Nairobi 12,000; Meru 7,000; Nairobi 8,500; Meru 3,500; Nairobi 4,500.

  1. By hand, Nairobi: 12,000 + 8,500 + 4,500 = 25,000.
  2. By hand, Meru: 7,000 + 3,500 = 10,500.
  3. Excel, with Region in B and Sales in C: =SUMIFS(C2:C6,B2:B6,"Nairobi") gives 25,000.
  4. Python: df.groupby("region")["sales"].sum() gives Meru 10,500 and Nairobi 25,000.
  5. Power BI: a bar visual of Region and Sales shows the same two bars.

Result: all routes agree and the grand total is 25,000 + 10,500 = 35,500.

Meaning: agreement is strong evidence that the calculation is right. If one differed, you would check filters, duplicates and blanks.

Concept checkExcel gives KES 25,000 for Nairobi but Python gives KES 29,500. What should you do?
Practitioner layer

One task, three tools. Task: total sales by region.

  • Excel: with Copilot where your Microsoft 365 plan offers it, ask "summarise sales by region". Or write =SUMIFS(Sales,Region,"Nairobi") yourself.
  • Power BI: drag Region and Sales to a bar visual, or use the Q&A visual: "total sales by region".
  • Python:
df.groupby("region")["sales"].sum()

All three should give identical totals. If they do not, find out why. That comparison is your best test of AI-written work.

Expert layer

AI features depend on your licence, version and settings, so check what is currently available to you before planning a workflow around them. The skill that transfers is knowing the logic: if you understand SUMIFS, groupby and DAX measures, you can verify any AI suggestion. Scikit-learn suits classic models on tables, while TensorFlow and transformers are for deep learning and language, and are heavier. Learn next: pick one tool and master it before spreading across all three.

Check yourself: You get the same regional totals from Excel, Power BI and Python. What does that tell you?

Answer: It is strong evidence that the calculation and the data handling are right, since three independent routes agree. If they differed, you would look for filters, duplicates or blank values.

slides.title: Real-World AI Use Cases
slides.content:
1. Sector – AI Application
  2. Healthcare – Predicting patient risk
  3. Retail – Personalizing product recommendations
  4. Finance – Fraud detection and credit scoring
  5. Agriculture – Crop yield forecasting
  6. Education – Adaptive learning and grading
  7. AI is reshaping industries.
  8. Analysts help design and interpret AI systems.
  9. Use cases show the power and responsibility of AI.
    10. Food for the Mind: AI is everywhere—your job is to make it meaningful.
Concept checkA team builds a fraud model on clean transaction data, but nobody is assigned to review the flagged transactions. What is the likely outcome?
Practitioner layer

Turn each use case into the question an analyst would ask:

SectorQuestionData needed
HealthWhich patients miss follow-up?Visit dates, ages, clinic
RetailWhat sells together?Receipt lines
FinanceWhich transactions look unusual?Amount, time, location
AgricultureWhat will a season yield?Rainfall, acreage, past harvests

Pick one row. Write the target you predict, the columns you need and one risk, such as missing rainfall records.

Expert layer

Every use case has the same three parts: a clear question, usable data, and a person who acts on the result. Where one is missing, the project fails, however clever the model. Look at the cost of mistakes: a wrong film recommendation is harmless, a wrong health or credit decision can hurt someone. Higher stakes mean more testing and human review. Analysts add value by defining the problem and judging results. Learn next: how to measure whether a model actually helped.

Check yourself: Pick one sector from the table and name the question, the data and the risk if the model is wrong.

Answer: For example, health: which patients will miss follow-up, using visit history, and the risk is that vulnerable patients are wrongly ignored or flagged unfairly.

slides.title: Limitations of AI
slides.content:
1. AI depends on the quality of data.
  2. It can’t understand context or emotion like humans.
  3. Models may be biased or inaccurate.
  4. Over-reliance can lead to blind decisions.
  5. Analysts must combine AI with human judgment.
    6. Food for the Mind: AI is smart—but not wise. That’s your role.
Concept checkYou ask a chatbot 'what was my shop's average basket size?' with no data and it replies confidently with a number. What does this show?
Practitioner layer

Test AI's limits yourself. Example: ask a tool "what was the average basket size at my shop?" without giving data. It may produce a confident number. That is a made-up answer. Now paste a dummy 10-row table and ask again; compute the average with =AVERAGE(C2:C11) and compare. Steps:

  1. Ask with no data. Note the answer.
  2. Ask with data.
  3. Check by hand.
  4. Record the gap.

Lesson: AI does not know your shop, your season or why sales dropped after a road closure. You supply the context.

Expert layer

Main limits: poor data gives poor output, models can be wrong yet sound sure, and they miss local context. A forecast built on one good year fails in a drought year. Over-reliance is subtle: you stop checking because it was right ten times. Keep a rule that important numbers need a second source. Never use AI output as the only basis for decisions about people, such as hiring or lending. Learn next: how to document assumptions in your report.

Check yourself: Why can an AI tool give a confident answer that is wrong?

Answer: It generates likely-sounding answers from patterns, not from verified knowledge of your data, so it can invent figures or miss context. That is why you check results against real data.

slides.title: Practical: Use AI in a Data Task
slides.content:
1. Task:
  2. Choose a dataset and use AI to clean, analyze, or visualize it.
  3. Try tools like ChatGPT, Copilot, or Python libraries.
  4. Document what AI did and what you reviewed manually.
  5. Reflect on how AI helped or hindered your process.
  6. Share your findings with a peer.
    7. Food for the Mind: Let AI assist—but make sure your fingerprints are on the final product.

Worked example: Logging an AI cleaning task

You have a dummy sheet of 200 shop sales rows with columns Date, Item, Qty, Price and Phone.

  1. Delete the Phone column before using any AI tool.
  2. Prompt: "Columns are Date, Item, Qty, Price_KES. Suggest pandas checks for duplicates, blanks and odd values."
  3. Run the code. It flags 12 duplicate rows.
  4. Check them yourself: 10 are true duplicates, 2 are separate sales at the same time.
  5. Remove the 10 true duplicates: 200 - 10 = 190 rows. Keep the other 2.

Log entry: AI flagged 12; I confirmed 10; rows before 200, after 190; raw file kept.

Meaning: the log shows what AI did, what you checked and where it was wrong, which is the real deliverable.

Concept checkAI flagged 12 duplicate rows. You checked and 10 were true duplicates; 2 were separate sales at the same time. What goes in your log?
Practitioner layer

Worked answer, using a dummy sheet of 200 shop sales rows (never real customer data in a public tool).

  1. Check the columns: Date, Item, Qty, Price, Phone. Delete Phone.
  2. Prompt: "Columns are Date, Item, Qty, Price_KES. Suggest checks for duplicates, blanks, and odd values, using pandas."
  3. Run the code, view the flagged rows.
  4. Fix by hand where you can explain it.
  5. Ask AI for a chart idea, build it yourself.
  6. Write a log: what AI did, what you checked, what you changed, what it got wrong.

Stretch: repeat with a second AI tool and compare the answers.

Expert layer

The log is the real deliverable. A strong log has rows such as: "AI said 12 duplicates, I found 10 true duplicates, 2 were separate sales at the same time". That shows judgement. Common slips: pasting real private data, accepting code you did not read, and forgetting the raw file. Save versions: raw, cleaned, final. When you share with a peer, ask them to find one thing you missed. Learn next: writing your steps as a reusable script.

Check yourself: What should your log record besides what the AI did?

Answer: What you reviewed and checked, what you changed or rejected and why, and where the AI was wrong or unhelpful.

slides.title: Q&A
slides.content:
1. What if AI gives wrong results? → Review and validate manually.
  2. What if I don’t understand the model? → Focus on inputs and outputs first.
  3. What if AI feels too complex? → Start with simple tools like Copilot or ChatGPT.
  4. What if I’m worried about bias? → Check your data and test fairness.
  5. What if I want to learn more? → Explore AI ethics, machine learning, and automation.
    6. Food for the Mind: AI is a tool—not a truth. Use it with care, and question everything.
Concept checkA colleague defends a number in a report by saying 'the AI said so'. What is the best response?
Practitioner layer

Q: What if AI gives wrong results? Test on a small sample with a known answer, compare with a manual calculation, and ask the tool to explain its steps.

Q: What if I do not understand the model? Describe inputs, outputs and one example. If you cannot explain why it gave a number, do not present it.

Q: Is it fine to paste my client's M-Pesa statements into a chatbot? No. Use anonymised or dummy rows, or an approved tool.

Q: How do I test for bias? Compare outcomes across groups, for example approval rates by gender or area, and investigate big gaps.

Expert layer

The best answer to most AI questions is a habit, not a tool: check small, verify against a second source, protect private data, write down what you did. If your organisation has rules on AI use, follow them, and ask when unsure. Do not argue with a model. Rephrase, add context and examples, and compare. Beginners often give too little detail; experts give columns, goals and constraints. Learn next: pick one real task per week and practise.

Check yourself: A colleague says "the AI said so" to justify a number in a report. How do you respond?

Answer: Ask how it was verified. Recalculate a sample by hand or in another tool, and only include the number once you can explain where it came from.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
slides.content:
1. AI enhances data analysis through automation and prediction.
  2. Tools like ChatGPT, Copilot, and Python libraries support analysts.
  3. Ethics and validation are critical in AI use.
  4. AI is powerful—but needs human guidance.
  5. You’re now equipped to use AI responsibly.
    6. Food for the Mind: AI gives you speed—your wisdom gives it direction.

Worked example: A four-part prompt, then a test

Write the prompt with role, context, task and format.

  1. Role: You are a data analyst helping a duka owner.
  2. Context: My table has Item in A and Qty in B.
  3. Task: write a SUMIFS formula for total Qty of Tea.
  4. Format: give the formula, then explain it in 2 lines.

Test it on a tiny table you can check by hand: Tea 4, Sugar 2, Tea 6 (rows 2 to 4).

By hand: 4 + 6 = 10.

Formula: =SUMIFS(B2:B4,A2:A4,"Tea") returns 10, which matches.

Meaning: you used a known answer to verify the AI draft before using it on real data, which is the habit that lasts.

Concept checkWhich sequence best describes a responsible AI workflow for a data task?
Practitioner layer

Consolidated model: AI = fast draft; you = question, data, check, judgement. Workflow: question, clean data, prompt with context, run, verify, explain, document.

Five-minute self-test:

  1. Name one analytics job AI can speed up.
  2. Write a four-part prompt for a SUMIFS formula.
  3. List two checks before trusting a cleaned dataset.
  4. What would you never paste into a public tool?
  5. How would you spot bias?

If any answer takes more than a minute, revisit that slide.

Expert layer

The mindset that lasts is verification. Tools will change names and features, so check what is currently available, but "test on known answers" works every time. Pro habit: keep your prompts, logs and checks as part of your portfolio, because they show how you think. Expect AI to handle more routine steps over time, which makes problem framing, domain knowledge and communication more valuable. Learn next: machine learning fundamentals and data protection.

Check yourself: Give the one-line workflow for using AI responsibly on a data task.

Answer: Define the question, clean the data, prompt with context (no private data), run and verify against known answers, explain the result, and document what you did.

slides.title: AI-Enhanced Analysis
slides.content:
1. Task:
  2. Choose a dataset and complete an analysis using AI tools.
  3. Use AI for cleaning, visualization, or prediction.
  4. Document your process and reflect on AI’s role.
  5. Share your project and insights.
  6. Save it for your portfolio.
    7. Food for the Mind: Your challenge is to lead the machine—don’t just use AI, guide it.

Worked example: Top five counties

Question: which five counties have the largest populations? Practice table (round, illustrative figures): Nairobi 4,400,000; Kiambu 2,400,000; Nakuru 2,200,000; Kakamega 1,900,000; Bungoma 1,700,000; Meru 1,500,000.

  1. Clean: check blanks and duplicates. None found, 6 rows.
  2. Analyse: df.nlargest(5, "population") returns Nairobi, Kiambu, Nakuru, Kakamega, Bungoma. Meru is left out.
  3. Check in Excel with the values in B2:B7: =LARGE(B2:B7,3) returns 2,200,000, the third largest, matching Nakuru.
  4. Chart: a sorted bar chart titled "Nairobi is the largest county, nearly twice Kiambu".

Check the title: 4,400,000 / 2,400,000 = 1.83, so "nearly twice" holds.

Meaning: two routes agree, and you document which step AI suggested.

Concept checkYou finish an AI-assisted analysis for your portfolio. What should the portfolio version include?
Practitioner layer

Full worked answer, using a free open dataset such as a public county population table.

  1. Question: which five counties have the largest populations?
  2. Clean: check blanks and duplicates (AI may suggest the code; you read it).
  3. Analyse: in pandas, df.nlargest(5, "population"), or Excel's =LARGE(B2:B48,1).
  4. Visualise: a bar chart sorted high to low, title stating the finding.
  5. Document: prompts used, outputs, your checks, errors found.
  6. Share in a one-page summary.

Stretch: add a second dataset and join them on county.

Expert layer

For a portfolio, process matters as much as result. Show the raw data, your question, three screenshots and a short note: "AI wrote this step, I changed this, here is why". Employers and clients trust people who can show verification. Avoid datasets with personal information. Check the licence and cite the source. Keep the project small and finished, rather than large and abandoned. Learn next: turn the same steps into a repeatable notebook or Power Query.

Check yourself: What belongs in the portfolio version of an AI-assisted analysis besides the final chart?

Answer: The question, data source, the steps you took, which parts AI did and which you checked or changed, and the limitations of the result.

slides.title: Lock It In: Module Recap
slides.content:
1. What is AI in Data Analytics?: AI refers to machines that mimic human intelligence—learning, reasoning, and decision-making.
  2. AI Tools for Analysts: ChatGPT helps generate summaries, explanations, and code.
  3. AI for Data Visualization: AI can suggest the best chart for your data.
  4. Predictive Analytics Basics: Predictive analytics uses historical data to forecast future outcomes.
  5. AI in Excel, Power BI, Python: Excel: Copilot suggests formulas and summaries.
  6. Real-World AI Use Cases: Healthcare – Predicting patient risk
  7. Practical: Use AI in a Data Task: Choose a dataset and use AI to clean, analyze, or visualize it.
  8. AI-Enhanced Analysis: Choose a dataset and complete an analysis using AI tools.
⭐ Activity: Close the lesson. Say each point above out loud in your own words, then give one example from your own life or work. Any point you cannot explain is where to go back and re-read.
Recall round (answer before you look)

Cover the answers. Say or write your answer to each question, then check yourself in the last layer below.

  1. Name the three branches of AI mentioned on this slide and give one analytics task for each. (from: What is AI in Data Analytics?)
  2. An AI tool deletes 300 rows it called outliers. What do you check before accepting this? (from: Automating Data Cleaning with AI)
  3. What is the difference between regression and classification, with one example of each? (from: Predictive Analytics Basics)
  4. You get the same regional totals from Excel, Power BI and Python. What does that tell you? (from: AI in Excel, Power BI, Python)
  5. Why can an AI tool give a confident answer that is wrong? (from: Limitations of AI)
  6. What belongs in the portfolio version of an AI-assisted analysis besides the final chart? (from: AI-Enhanced Analysis)
Teach it back
  1. Explain the three ideas you find hardest to a friend or family member in two minutes, without notes.
  2. Wherever you stumble, write the lesson name down and go back to it. Re-read the Practice layer and redo the activity.
  3. This week, use one idea from this module in real life or work, and note what happened.
  4. Come back in two days and answer the recall questions again. Remembering after a gap is what makes it stay.

Lessons to revisit if needed:

  • What is AI in Data Analytics?
  • AI Tools for Analysts
  • AI for Data Visualization
  • Predictive Analytics Basics
  • AI in Excel, Power BI, Python
  • Real-World AI Use Cases
  • Practical: Use AI in a Data Task
  • AI-Enhanced Analysis
Check yourself: the answers

Answers, in the same order:

  1. Machine learning (predicting sales from past sales), natural language processing (grouping customer comments into themes), computer vision (reading text or counting items from photos of receipts or shelves).
  2. Look at the deleted rows to see whether they are errors or real unusual cases, compare row counts and totals before and after, and keep the raw file. Record your decision in a cleaning log.
  3. Regression predicts a number, such as next month's sales in KES. Classification predicts a category, such as whether a loan will be repaid or defaulted.
  4. It is strong evidence that the calculation and the data handling are right, since three independent routes agree. If they differed, you would look for filters, duplicates or blank values.
  5. It generates likely-sounding answers from patterns, not from verified knowledge of your data, so it can invent figures or miss context. That is why you check results against real data.
  6. The question, data source, the steps you took, which parts AI did and which you checked or changed, and the limitations of the result.

title: Trends & The Future of Data Analytics

slides.title: The Evolving Data Landscape
slides.content:
1. Data is growing exponentially—volume, variety, and velocity.
  2. New sources include IoT, social media, and real-time sensors.
  3. Analysts must adapt to faster, more complex data environments.
  4. Cloud platforms and AI are reshaping workflows.
  5. The future is real-time, predictive, and automated.
    6. Food for the Mind: Data never sleeps—stay curious, stay current.
Concept checkA shop in Nanyuki records 150 sales a day in one Excel file, updated once each evening. What is the best tool choice?
Practitioner layer

Three Vs in numbers: volume (how many rows), variety (tables, text, images), velocity (how fast new data arrives). Example: a supermarket gets 5,000 till receipts a day (volume), plus M-Pesa logs and CCTV counts (variety), updating every minute (velocity). Excel copes with the first; the others need databases, scripts or cloud tools.

Check yourself: for your own project, ask how many rows today, how many file types, and how often it refreshes. If all three are small, Excel or SQLite is fine.

Expert layer

New does not mean better. Pick the simplest tool that handles your data. Excel's row limit is just over a million per sheet, and a messy folder of files is a bigger problem than size. Real-time dashboards sound exciting but cost effort, so ask whether the decision truly needs minute-by-minute data. Pro habit: learn the foundations (SQL, data cleaning, statistics) because they carry over to every new platform. Learn next: databases and basic cloud ideas.

Check yourself: A shop gets 200 sales a day. Does it need big data tools? Explain.

Answer: Probably not. Volume is small, so Excel, SQLite or a simple database is enough. Big data tools matter when volume, variety or speed outgrow ordinary tools.

slides.title: Big Data & Cloud Analytics
slides.content:
1. Big Data refers to massive datasets that traditional tools can’t handle.
  2. Cloud platforms like Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud offer scalable solutions.
  3. Analysts use cloud tools for storage, processing, and collaboration.
  4. Cloud analytics enables remote access and real-time updates.
  5. Learn to work with cloud-based data pipelines.
    6. Food for the Mind: The cloud is your playground—big data, big possibilities.
Concept checkA pharmacy chain stores daily sales in a cloud database. A manager at one branch wants to see totals without emailing files. What should be set up?
Practitioner layer

Cloud analytics means data and processing live on remote servers you reach through the internet. A simple example: a chain of pharmacies saves daily sales to a cloud database; a manager opens a Power BI report from any branch.

  1. Store: files or tables in cloud storage.
  2. Process: SQL or scripts clean and combine them.
  3. Share: a dashboard refreshes on a schedule.

Try it free: upload a CSV to Google Sheets or Looker Studio, build a chart, share a view-only link. Notice that the data is no longer on your laptop only.

Expert layer

Cloud brings convenience and new risks: cost that grows with use, access that must be controlled, and data stored in someone else's data centre. Check who may see the data and where it is kept, particularly for personal or health data. Cloud platforms keep changing, so learn the concepts (storage, compute, pipelines, permissions) and the product names will follow. Pro habit: set spending limits and turn off what you do not use. Learn next: SQL, then one cloud tool.

Check yourself: Name the three stages in the simple cloud pipeline above and what each does.

Answer: Store (keep data in cloud files or tables), process (clean and combine with SQL or scripts), share (dashboards or reports that refresh on a schedule).

slides.title: Data Science vs. Data Analytics
slides.content:
1. Role: Data Analyst – Descriptive & diagnostic analysis
  2. Role: Data Scientist – Predictive & prescriptive modeling
  3. Analysts explain what happened and why.
  4. Scientists predict what will happen and how to optimize it.
  5. Both roles require strong data skills.
  6. Analysts often transition into data science.
  7. Choose your path based on interest and goals.
    8. Food for the Mind: Analytics tells the story—data science writes the sequel.

Worked example: sorting a boutique's questions

Wanjiru runs a boutique in Meru. Her December sales were KES 120,000 and January sales were KES 90,000. She asks four questions.

  1. Which dresses sold best in December? This looks at the past, so it is descriptive.
  2. How big was the fall? 120,000 - 90,000 = 30,000, and 30,000 / 120,000 = 0.25, so sales fell 25%. This is still descriptive.
  3. Why did sales fall in January? She checks school fees season and stock-outs. This explains the past, so it is diagnostic.
  4. How many will we sell in March? This estimates the future, so it is predictive.

A fifth question, what stock level maximises profit, would be prescriptive.

Result: the first three need SQL, Excel and charts. The last two need statistics and modelling.

Concept checkA boutique owner asks: 'How many dresses should we order for March to make the most profit?' Which type of question is this?
Practitioner layer

The sentence to remember: analysts mostly ask what happened and why; scientists often ask what will happen. Example with a boutique:

QuestionType
Which dresses sold best in December?Descriptive
Why did sales fall in January?Diagnostic
How many will we sell in March?Predictive
What stock level maximises profit?Prescriptive

Mark which skills each needs: SQL and charts for the first two; statistics and modelling for the last two.

Expert layer

The lines blur. Many analyst jobs include simple forecasting, and many data science jobs are mostly cleaning. Titles vary between employers, so read the description, not the title. Moving towards data science means adding statistics, Python, and model testing on top of strong analyst skills. You do not need to decide now: pick the work that you enjoy and keep strengthening fundamentals. Learn next: descriptive statistics, then simple regression.

Check yourself: Classify as descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or prescriptive: "Why did clinic visits drop in April?"

Answer: Diagnostic, because it asks why something that already happened occurred.

slides.title: Data Engineering Basics
slides.content:
1. Data engineers build systems to collect, store, and move data.
  2. They design pipelines and manage databases.
  3. Tools include SQL, Python, Spark, and cloud platforms.
  4. Analysts often work with engineers to access clean data.
  5. Understanding engineering helps analysts collaborate better.
    6. Food for the Mind: Engineers build the roads—analysts drive the insights.
Concept checkA nightly pipeline copies a pharmacy's sales CSV into a table, but duplicate rows keep appearing in reports. Which ETL step should fix this?
Practitioner layer

A data pipeline moves data from source to a place where analysts can use it. Example: a pharmacy system exports daily sales.

  1. Extract: copy the CSV from the system every night.
  2. Transform: remove duplicates, fix date formats, add a product category.
  3. Load: insert into a database table.

A tiny version in SQL:

INSERT INTO sales_clean (sale_date, item, qty)
SELECT DISTINCT sale_date, item, qty
FROM sales_raw;

This pattern is called ETL (extract, transform, load). The analyst then queries sales_clean.

Expert layer

Pipelines break quietly: a column renamed, a file missing, a date format changed. Good engineers add checks such as row counts and alerts. As an analyst, ask three questions of any dataset you receive: where does it come from, how often is it updated, and who owns it? Document your own queries so others can rerun them. Learn next: SQL joins, scheduled refreshes in Power BI, and basic Python scripting.

Check yourself: What do the letters in ETL stand for, and which step would remove duplicates?

Answer: Extract, transform, load. Removing duplicates happens in the transform step.

slides.title: Data Analytics in Kenya & Africa
slides.content:
1. Governments use data for planning, budgeting, and service delivery.
  2. Businesses use analytics for customer insights and growth.
  3. NGOs use data to measure impact and allocate resources.
  4. Mobile money and agriculture are key data-rich sectors.
  5. Africa’s data future is local, innovative, and community-driven.
    6. Food for the Mind: Kenya’s data story is rising—be part of the movement.
Concept checkA SACCO keeps loan repayments on paper and in inconsistent spellings. What is the most useful first contribution of a local analyst?
Practitioner layer

Turn the slide into a practical local task: pick a data-rich sector and sketch one analysis.

Example: a small SACCO records loan repayments each month.

  1. Question: which month has the most late repayments?
  2. Data: member ID, due date, paid date.
  3. Calculation: =IF(C2>B2,1,0) flags late payments; a PivotTable counts them by month.
  4. Action: send reminders before that month.

Mobile money transactions, farm records and clinic registers all work the same way, but always check who owns the data and whether people agreed to its use.

Expert layer

Local data work has local challenges: records kept on paper, inconsistent spellings of place names, gaps in rural coverage, and strict care needed around personal data. These are chances for analysts who can clean and standardise carefully. Do not assume global solutions fit directly; talk to the people who collect the data. Public sources such as the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics and the Kenya Open Data portal are good practice material. Learn next: the Data Protection Act basics.

Check yourself: Why can a local analyst add value even before using advanced models?

Answer: Because many local datasets are messy or on paper, and careful cleaning, standardising and clear reporting turn them into usable decisions. This depends on understanding the local context.

slides.title: Industry Trends (Finance, Health, etc.)
slides.content:
1. Sector: Finance – Real-time fraud detection
  2. Sector: Health – Predictive patient care
  3. Sector: Retail – Personalized marketing
  4. Sector: Education – Learning analytics
  5. Sector: Agriculture – Smart farming with sensors
  6. Each industry uses data differently.
  7. Analysts must understand domain-specific needs.
  8. Trends include automation, personalization, and prediction.
  9. Stay updated through blogs, webinars, and reports.
  10. Choose a sector that aligns with your passion.
    11. Food for the Mind: Every industry speaks data—learn its dialect, lead its future.
Concept checkAn analyst builds a flawless chart of 'visits per clinic' for a retail shop owner who wants to know which products earn the most. What went wrong?
Practitioner layer

To learn a sector's "dialect", write a mini glossary and the core measures it uses:

SectorKey measures
RetailGross margin, stock turnover
HealthVisits per clinic, follow-up rate
FinanceDefault rate, repayment time
AgricultureYield per acre

Example: gross margin % = (Sales - Cost) / Sales. Sales KES 10,000, cost KES 7,000 gives 30%. Choose one sector, list 5 terms with plain definitions, and find one public dataset.

Expert layer

Trends are signals, but domain knowledge makes analysis useful. A technically correct chart with the wrong measure wastes everyone's time. Talk to people who work in the sector and ask what decisions they make weekly. Be careful with blogs and webinars: check the date and the source, and see if claims are backed by data. Choosing a sector is not permanent; skills in cleaning, SQL and visualisation move between them. Learn next: pick a sector and build one small project.

Check yourself: Why does an analyst need to learn sector vocabulary as well as tools?

Answer: Because choosing the right measure and interpreting results depends on how the sector works. Correct formulas applied to the wrong measure still mislead decision makers.

slides.title: Data Privacy & Security
slides.content:
1. Data must be protected from misuse and breaches.
  2. Privacy laws like GDPR and Kenya’s Data Protection Act matter.
  3. Analysts must handle sensitive data responsibly.
  4. Use encryption, access controls, and anonymization.
  5. Ethics and security go hand in hand.
    6. Food for the Mind: Trust is built on privacy—protect the data, protect the people.
Concept checkYou must share a clinic's patient list. You drop name and phone, but keep exact age, village and diagnosis. What is the best next step?
Practitioner layer

Three habits protect data in daily work. Example: you hold a clinic's patient list.

  1. Minimise: drop columns you do not need (name, phone, ID number).
  2. Anonymise: replace the patient name with a code. In Excel: a helper column with ="P"&TEXT(ROW()-1,"0000") gives P0001, P0002. Keep the key linking codes to names in a separate, locked file.
  3. Restrict: password-protect the file and share only with named people.

Then ask: would a stranger be able to identify someone from age, village and diagnosis together? If yes, group ages into bands.

Expert layer

Removing names is not always enough: a few combined details can point to one person. Always ask who collected the data, what consent covers, and who may see results. Kenya's Data Protection Act sets duties for handling personal data, so find out your organisation's policy and, for real projects, ask a qualified person where unsure. Never email raw personal data casually or paste it into public AI tools. Pro habit: delete working copies when finished. Learn next: data governance basics.

Check yourself: Why might a dataset without names still identify a patient?

Answer: Combinations such as age, village, date and diagnosis can point to one person. Grouping values into bands and sharing fewer details reduces that risk.

slides.title: Open Data & Collaboration
slides.content:
1. Open data is free, public, and reusable.
  2. Governments and NGOs publish datasets for transparency.
  3. Collaboration leads to innovation and shared solutions.
  4. Use platforms like Kenya Open Data and World Bank.
  5. Open data empowers communities and drives change.
    6. Food for the Mind: Open data is open opportunity—share, learn, and build together.
Concept checkYou download a county-level CSV from an open data portal. Before using it in a report, what is the best habit?
Practitioner layer

Open data is only useful if you can load and check it. Practice with a public table, for example a county-level CSV from Kenya Open Data or the World Bank.

  1. Download the CSV and note the source, date and licence.
  2. Open in Excel: Data tab, From Text/CSV.
  3. Check the column headings, units and missing values.
  4. Make one chart.
  5. Write a source line under it: "Source: [portal name], downloaded [date]".

In Python: pd.read_csv("file.csv") then df.info() shows types and blanks.

Expert layer

Free does not mean perfect. Open datasets can be old, revised, or defined differently from what you assume; read the notes or metadata file before you analyse. Respect licences and give credit. Collaboration works when you share clean code and documentation along with results, so others can reproduce your work. When you publish, never include personal data. Pro habit: save the original download untouched. Learn next: joining two open datasets by a common key like county.

Check yourself: List three things to record when you use an open dataset.

Answer: The source, the download date or version, and the licence or usage terms. Notes on units and definitions are also useful.

slides.title: Building a Career in Analytics
slides.content:
1. Start with strong foundations in tools and thinking.
  2. Build a portfolio with real projects.
  3. Network through meetups, LinkedIn, and online forums.
  4. Stay updated with certifications and courses.
  5. Choose a niche and grow your expertise.
    6. Food for the Mind: Your career is a journey—every dataset is a step forward.

Worked example: a duka profit project

Kamau wants a portfolio project that answers: which items give his duka the most profit this week?

  1. Question: which item earns the most profit?
  2. Data: units sold times profit per unit. Sugar: 50 x KES 20 = 1,000. Bread: 100 x KES 5 = 500. Milk: 40 x KES 8 = 320.
  3. Total profit: 1,000 + 500 + 320 = 1,820.
  4. Sugar share: 1,000 / 1,820 = 0.549, about 55%.
  5. Chart: a bar chart of profit by item.

Finding: sugar earns the most profit, even though bread sells more units. Next step: check whether sugar stock runs out mid-week.

He puts the question, method, chart, finding and next step on one page. That is visible proof of skill for the portfolio.

Concept checkA learner has ten half-finished analyses and no write-ups. A friend advises how to build a career portfolio. Which advice fits best?
Practitioner layer

A career is built from visible proof. Use a simple 4-step plan:

  1. Foundations: Excel, SQL, one visual tool, basic statistics.
  2. Projects: three small projects, each answering a real question, such as "Which items give a duka the most profit?"
  3. Show: put each on a one-page write-up with the question, method, chart, finding and what you would do next.
  4. Connect: share your work, ask for feedback, offer to help a small business or community group with a free sample analysis.

Review your list every month and fill the weakest gap.

Expert layer

Nobody can promise outcomes, and the job market changes, so build skills that are useful in many settings. Quality beats quantity: three clear, honest projects are stronger than ten half-finished ones. Be ready to explain every number you present. Learn the vocabulary of one sector. Courses and certifications can help, but check what a programme really teaches. Pro habit: keep a learning log and a list of questions you can now answer. Learn next: pick a niche and build a deeper project.

Check yourself: What should each portfolio project one-pager contain?

Answer: The question, the data and method, a clear chart, the finding, and what action you would recommend or what you would do next.

slides.title: Practical: Research a Trend
slides.content:
1. Task:
  2. Choose a trend in data analytics (e.g., AI, cloud, open data).
  3. Research how it’s used in Kenya or globally.
  4. Write a short summary with examples and impact.
  5. Share your findings with the class or mentor.
  6. Reflect on how this trend affects your future.
    7. Food for the Mind: Trends are signals—follow them to shape your path.
Concept checkAn AI tool gives you three sources for your trend summary. What is the right way to use them?
Practitioner layer

Use a short research method to avoid vague summaries. Example topic: mobile money data.

  1. Narrow: "How is data analytics used with mobile payments by small traders in Kenya?"
  2. Find 3 sources: a news article, an organisation report, a case study. Note the date.
  3. Extract: what data, what method, what decision changed.
  4. Write 200 words: trend, example, impact, limits.
  5. Check claims: is each number traceable to a source?

Stretch: try a small analysis with a public dataset on the same trend.

Expert layer

Beware hype. Treat claims without a named source and date with caution, and do not repeat numbers you cannot trace. Compare at least two viewpoints. A strong summary says what is happening, who it helps, who might be harmed, and what evidence is weak. If you use AI to find sources, open each source yourself, since tools can invent references. Present findings in plain language. Learn next: turning a trend summary into a skill plan, as the next task does.

Check yourself: Why should you open every source yourself if an AI tool suggested it?

Answer: AI tools can produce references that do not exist or misstate what a source says, so you must confirm the source is real and supports the claim.

slides.title: Q&A
slides.content:
1. What if I don’t know which trend to follow? → Explore and experiment.
  2. What if I’m worried about automation? → Focus on skills that AI can’t replace.
  3. What if I want to work in Kenya? → Learn local tools, laws, and needs.
  4. What if I’m interested in multiple sectors? → Start broad, then specialize.
  5. What if I feel behind? → The future is still being written—start now.
    6. Food for the Mind: The future isn’t fixed—it’s yours to shape.
Concept checkAmina is worried about falling behind and keeps switching between new tools every week. What advice fits the lesson?
Practitioner layer

Q: Which trend should I follow? Pick one connected to work you can do now, for example SQL plus dashboards, and try a small project.

Q: Will automation take my job? Routine tasks get automated. Skills in defining questions, knowing the business, checking quality and explaining results stay valuable. No one can predict exactly, so keep learning.

Q: I want to work locally, what do I learn? Data protection rules, local sector knowledge, and tools your target employers use.

Q: How do I stop feeling behind? Practise one skill weekly and finish small projects.

Expert layer

Fear of falling behind pushes people to jump between tools. Do the opposite: depth first. Strong fundamentals make new tools easy to learn. Ask people working in your target field what they actually use, and look at several job descriptions to find common skills. Do not trust anyone who promises a guaranteed income from a single course. Keep a short list of next skills and review monthly. Learn next: choose one project that combines two skills you already have.

Check yourself: A learner is interested in three sectors. What practical advice would you give?

Answer: Start with the shared fundamentals (Excel, SQL, visuals, statistics), build one small project in each sector, then specialise in the one where you enjoy the questions and find data.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
slides.content:
1. Data analytics is evolving with AI, cloud, and big data.
  2. Analysts must adapt to new tools and trends.
  3. Kenya and Africa offer unique opportunities.
  4. Ethics, privacy, and collaboration matter.
  5. You’re ready to build a future-proof career.
    6. Food for the Mind: You’re not just learning data—you’re learning to lead with it.

Worked example: the same workflow on a new tool

Njeri sells clothes online and moves to a new dashboard tool. Her workflow does not change.

  1. Question: what were total sales this week?
  2. Data: five sales in KES: 1,200; 950; 950; 2,000; 1,500.
  3. Clean: the two 950 rows share one receipt number, so it is a duplicate. Remove one.
  4. Analyse: raw total 1,200 + 950 + 950 + 2,000 + 1,500 = 6,600. Clean total 1,200 + 950 + 2,000 + 1,500 = 5,650.
  5. Visualise: a simple bar chart of sales per day.
  6. Communicate: "Sales were KES 5,650, not 6,600; a duplicate was removed."
  7. Protect: show customer codes, not names or phone numbers.

The duplicate would have overstated sales by KES 950 (6,600 - 5,650).

Concept checkA new analytics platform replaces your old tool. Which part of your approach should stay the same?
Practitioner layer

Consolidated model: tools change, the workflow stays: question, data, clean, analyse, visualise, communicate, protect people.

Five-minute self-test:

  1. Name the three Vs of big data.
  2. Give one example each of descriptive and predictive questions.
  3. What does ETL mean?
  4. Name two steps to protect personal data.
  5. Where would you find open data for Kenya?

If you hesitate on one, reopen that slide and write a two-line answer in your own words. Then plan one trend and one skill to learn next.

Expert layer

Strong analysts keep three loops running: learn a little each week, practise on real data, and talk to the people who use the answers. Trends are useful only when linked to a decision someone must make. Be sceptical of big claims and do not rely on one source. Protect privacy by default. Your best long-term advantage is the ability to explain results simply and honestly. Learn next: write your 30-day plan on the following task.

Check yourself: State the workflow that stays the same even when tools change.

Answer: Ask the question, gather and clean the data, analyse, visualise, communicate the finding, and protect the people behind the data.

slides.title: Future-Proof Your Skills
slides.content:
1. Task:
  2. Choose one trend and one skill to focus on next.
  3. Create a 30-day learning plan with resources and goals.
  4. Join a community or attend a webinar.
  5. Reflect on how this will grow your career.
  6. Share your plan with a peer or mentor.
    7. Food for the Mind: Your challenge is to grow forward—learn what lasts, lead what’s next.

Worked example: a 30-day SQL plan

Achieng picks one trend (cloud dashboards) and one skill (SQL). She studies 30 minutes a day on 5 days a week.

  1. Week 1: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY on a practice table.
  2. Week 2: GROUP BY and aggregates.
  3. Week 3: JOINs on two tables.
  4. Week 4: build one dashboard from SQL results and share it.

Time per week: 30 x 5 = 150 minutes. Over 4 weeks: 150 x 4 = 600 minutes, and 600 / 60 = 10 hours.

Her days: 4 weeks x 5 study days = 20 days. The other 10 of the 30 days include rest and a catch-up day for a bad week. Each week ends with something she can show, and at day 30 she reviews what worked and what to drop.

Concept checkMwangi wants to learn Python, cloud dashboards, Power BI, machine learning and SQL in 30 days. What should a good plan do?
Practitioner layer

Worked 30-day plan. Trend: cloud dashboards. Skill: SQL.

WeekGoal
1SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY on a practice table
2GROUP BY and aggregates
3JOINs on two tables
4Build one dashboard from SQL results and share it

Each week: 30 minutes a day, one small exercise, one note on what confused you. Join one community or webinar, and write down one question to ask. Share the plan with a peer and agree a check-in date.

Stretch: add a measurable end goal, such as "answer 10 questions from a public dataset".

Expert layer

Plans fail when they are too big. Choose one trend and one skill only, and make each week end with something you can show. Use free or low-cost resources you have checked yourself. Expect a bad week and plan a catch-up day. Review at day 30: what worked, what to drop, what next. Reflecting on career growth is more honest when you note evidence (projects done) instead of hopes. Learn next: repeat the cycle with the next skill on your list.

Check yourself: Why choose only one trend and one skill for a 30-day plan?

Answer: A narrow focus makes the plan realistic and lets you produce something visible by day 30. Too many goals usually lead to none finished.

slides.title: Lock It In: Module Recap
slides.content:
1. The Evolving Data Landscape: Data is growing exponentially—volume, variety, and velocity.
  2. Big Data & Cloud Analytics: Big Data refers to massive datasets that traditional tools can’t handle.
  3. Data Engineering Basics: Data engineers build systems to collect, store, and move data.
  4. Data Analytics in Kenya & Africa: Governments use data for planning, budgeting, and service delivery.
  5. Data Privacy & Security: Data must be protected from misuse and breaches.
  6. Open Data & Collaboration: Open data is free, public, and reusable.
  7. Practical: Research a Trend: Choose a trend in data analytics (e.g., AI, cloud, open data).
  8. Future-Proof Your Skills: Choose one trend and one skill to focus on next.
⭐ Activity: Close the lesson. Say each point above out loud in your own words, then give one example from your own life or work. Any point you cannot explain is where to go back and re-read.
Recall round (answer before you look)

Cover the answers. Say or write your answer to each question, then check yourself in the last layer below.

  1. A shop gets 200 sales a day. Does it need big data tools? Explain. (from: The Evolving Data Landscape)
  2. Classify as descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or prescriptive: "Why did clinic visits drop in April?" (from: Data Science vs. Data Analytics)
  3. Why can a local analyst add value even before using advanced models? (from: Data Analytics in Kenya & Africa)
  4. Why might a dataset without names still identify a patient? (from: Data Privacy & Security)
  5. What should each portfolio project one-pager contain? (from: Building a Career in Analytics)
  6. Why choose only one trend and one skill for a 30-day plan? (from: Future-Proof Your Skills)
Teach it back
  1. Explain the three ideas you find hardest to a friend or family member in two minutes, without notes.
  2. Wherever you stumble, write the lesson name down and go back to it. Re-read the Practice layer and redo the activity.
  3. This week, use one idea from this module in real life or work, and note what happened.
  4. Come back in two days and answer the recall questions again. Remembering after a gap is what makes it stay.

Lessons to revisit if needed:

  • The Evolving Data Landscape
  • Big Data & Cloud Analytics
  • Data Engineering Basics
  • Data Analytics in Kenya & Africa
  • Data Privacy & Security
  • Open Data & Collaboration
  • Practical: Research a Trend
  • Future-Proof Your Skills
Check yourself: the answers

Answers, in the same order:

  1. Probably not. Volume is small, so Excel, SQLite or a simple database is enough. Big data tools matter when volume, variety or speed outgrow ordinary tools.
  2. Diagnostic, because it asks why something that already happened occurred.
  3. Because many local datasets are messy or on paper, and careful cleaning, standardising and clear reporting turn them into usable decisions. This depends on understanding the local context.
  4. Combinations such as age, village, date and diagnosis can point to one person. Grouping values into bands and sharing fewer details reduces that risk.
