  5. The question, the data and method, a clear chart, the finding, and what action you would recommend or what you would do next.
  6. A narrow focus makes the plan realistic and lets you produce something visible by day 30. Too many goals usually lead to none finished.

slides.title: Welcome: Learn to Think Like a Business Intelligence Consultant
slides.content:
Welcome to Module 14. This module teaches you how to move beyond creating charts and become someone who can investigate a business, explain what its numbers mean and recommend what management should do.

You do not need to know everything before you begin. Start with the first lesson, follow the examples, attempt each question and use the explanations to correct your thinking.

1. Understand

Learn the business problem in plain language.

2. Investigate

Know which records and metrics to examine.

3. Explain

Interpret the evidence and its limitations.

4. Recommend

Connect findings to a practical action.

How to use this module: Read each slide in order. Do the worked example yourself before revealing or comparing the explanation. In each knowledge check, select an answer. You will receive immediate feedback. You can revisit any slide using the sidebar.

Concept checkWanjiru sends the owner a bar chart of monthly sales and nothing else. What would a consultant add?
Practitioner layer
  1. Read the slides in order and keep a notebook beside you.
  2. Before you read each worked example, try the calculation yourself.
  3. Answer each knowledge check, then read the feedback even if you were right.
  4. Finish every slide’s “Check yourself” before moving on.
Expert layer

A chart-maker shows numbers. A consultant explains what the numbers mean, what is still unknown and what the owner should do next. Throughout this module, practise saying “the data shows… but it does not yet show…”.

Check yourself: In your own words, what is the difference between making a chart and consulting?

Answer: A chart shows the data. A consultant investigates, explains the meaning and limits of the evidence, and recommends a practical action.

slides.title: Before You Start: Essential Business Language
slides.content:
Business analysis becomes easier when you understand the language used by business owners and managers.

  • Revenue: money earned from selling goods or services before subtracting costs.
  • Cost of goods sold (COGS): the direct cost of the goods that were actually sold.
  • Gross profit: revenue minus COGS.
  • Operating expenses: costs of running the business, such as rent, salaries, internet and utilities.
  • Net profit: what remains after all relevant expenses have been deducted.
  • Cash flow: money entering and leaving the business. Profit and cash are not the same thing.
  • Inventory: goods held for sale.
  • KPI: key performance indicator; a measure used to monitor an important business objective.
Concept checkA shop shows KSh 150,000 profit but the owner has no cash. Which explanation fits the lesson?
Practitioner layer

Mini example: sales KSh 1,000, COGS KSh 600, operating expenses KSh 250.

  1. Gross profit = 1,000 − 600 = KSh 400.
  2. Net profit (before tax and interest) = 400 − 250 = KSh 150.
  3. Gross margin = 400 ÷ 1,000 = 40%.
Expert layer

Profit and cash are different. A business can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash if customers pay late, stock is bought in bulk, loans are repaid or the owner withdraws money. Always ask for both a profit view and a cash view.

Check yourself: A shop shows a KSh 150,000 profit but has no cash. Give one possible reason.

Answer: Examples: customers have not paid yet, cash was spent on extra stock, a loan was repaid, or the owner withdrew money. Profit is not the same as cash.

slides.title: The Consultant’s Investigation Method
slides.content:
Use this same sequence whenever a business owner brings you a problem. Do not jump straight into Power BI or Python.

  1. Clarify the question. What does the owner mean by “we are losing money” or “sales are poor”?
  2. Define the measure. Agree on what counts as a sale, cost, return, customer or month.
  3. Request source records. Obtain the relevant transaction, stock, expense or customer data.
  4. Check data quality. Look for missing records, duplicates, inconsistent dates and incorrect values.
  5. Calculate and compare. Compare periods, products, branches or targets fairly.
  6. Investigate causes. Separate what the data proves from what still needs checking.
  7. Recommend an action. State who should do what, why, and how success will be measured.

Worked example: Clarifying "sales are poor"

Mercy runs a pharmacy in Meru and says "sales are poor". You follow the method.

  1. Clarify: poor compared with what? She means January's target of KSh 500,000.
  2. Define: sales means shillings invoiced, excluding returns. Agree this in one sentence before opening any data.
  3. Request and check: January invoices plus last year's. No duplicates found.
  4. Calculate: invoiced KSh 400,000. Target achievement = 400,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 80%.
  5. Compare fairly: last January was KSh 450,000. Change = 400,000 − 450,000 = −50,000, and −50,000 ÷ 450,000 = −11.1%.

Result: sales are 20% below target and 11.1% below last year. Meaning: her feeling is supported, but the data does not yet show which products or weeks caused it. Next, split by product and week before recommending anything.

Concept checkAn owner says "sales are poor". What should you do before opening Power BI or Excel?
Practitioner layer

Apply the method to the sentence “sales are poor”:

  1. Clarify: poor compared with what? Last month, last year or the target?
  2. Define: do sales mean orders, shillings received or shillings invoiced?
  3. Request: sales records for 12 months, by product and branch.
  4. Check quality, calculate, then investigate causes before recommending.
Expert layer

Write the question and the definition in one sentence before you open any data. If the owner cannot agree the definition, you will later argue about the numbers instead of the business.

Check yourself: Why should you define a measure before calculating it?

Answer: Because different definitions give different answers. Agreeing the definition first stops later disputes about the numbers.

slides.title: Business Problem 1: Selling More but Earning Less — Understand the Problem
slides.content:
What this means: Revenue is the total value of sales. Profit is what remains after costs. A business can sell more units and still make less profit if purchase costs, discounts, returns or operating expenses rise.

Why a business owner should care
Owners often judge the business by how much it sells. If the margin shrinks, every extra shilling of sales brings in less profit, so growth can quietly drain cash.

The key measure: Gross profit = Revenue − COGS. Gross margin % = Gross profit ÷ Revenue × 100.

Worked example: Margin falling while sales grow

Kamau's shop sold more in February but he feels poorer. Check the margin.

  1. January: revenue 400,000, COGS 280,000. Gross profit = 400,000 − 280,000 = 120,000. Margin = 120,000 ÷ 400,000 × 100 = 30%.
  2. February: revenue 520,000, COGS 416,000. Gross profit = 520,000 − 416,000 = 104,000. Margin = 104,000 ÷ 520,000 × 100 = 20%.
  3. Revenue change = (520,000 − 400,000) ÷ 400,000 × 100 = 30%.
  4. Gross profit change = (104,000 − 120,000) ÷ 120,000 × 100 = −13.3%.

Result: revenue rose 30% but gross profit fell by KSh 16,000. Meaning: each shilling of sales kept 20 cents instead of 30. This is the warning sign of selling more but earning less. The numbers do not yet show whether discounts, costs or product mix caused it.

Concept checkA shop's revenue rose but its gross margin fell, and no prices were changed. What could explain this?
Practitioner layer — how to spot it

How to spot it in the records:

  1. Calculate gross profit and gross margin for each month, not revenue alone.
  2. Compare the margin percentages. A falling margin with rising sales is the warning sign.
  3. Split the result by product to see which items pulled the margin down.
  4. Check discounts and returns for the same period.
Expert layer

Margin can fall even when no price changed, simply because customers bought more of the low-margin products. This is called a mix effect. Compare product-level margins before blaming suppliers or staff.

Check yourself: Revenue rose 30% but gross profit fell. What does that tell you about the margin?

Answer: The gross margin fell (from 30% to 20% in the example). Each shilling of sales kept less profit.

slides.title: Business Problem 1: Selling More but Earning Less — Worked Example
slides.content:
Follow the numbers slowly. Write down the formula, substitute the values and calculate the result.

Worked example

A shop records revenue of KSh 500,000 and COGS of KSh 350,000. Gross profit is 500,000 − 350,000 = KSh 150,000. If next month revenue rises to KSh 650,000 but COGS rises to KSh 520,000, gross profit becomes KSh 130,000. Revenue increased by 30%, but gross profit fell by 13.3%. Gross margin also fell from 30% to 20%.

Interpretation

In month one, each shilling of sales left 30 cents of gross profit. In month two it left only 20 cents. The extra sales were bought with a lower margin. Possible causes are discounts, higher supplier prices or a shift towards low-margin products. The numbers show that this happened; they do not yet show why.

Concept checkJanuary: revenue 400,000, COGS 300,000. February: revenue 500,000, COGS 400,000. Which statement is correct?
Practitioner layer — redo it

Redo the calculation yourself:

  1. Write the formulas: gross profit = revenue − COGS; margin = gross profit ÷ revenue.
  2. Month 1: 500,000 − 350,000 = 150,000, and 150,000 ÷ 500,000 = 30%.
  3. Month 2: 650,000 − 520,000 = 130,000, and 130,000 ÷ 650,000 = 20%.
  4. Change in gross profit: (130,000 − 150,000) ÷ 150,000 = −13.3%.
Expert layer

Two different questions hide here. Did costs per unit rise (supplier price), or did prices per unit fall (discounts)? Separate price effect from cost effect from mix effect before recommending action.

Check yourself: Revenue 800,000 and COGS 560,000. What are the gross profit and gross margin?

Answer: Gross profit KSh 240,000 and gross margin 30% (240,000 ÷ 800,000).

slides.title: Business Problem 1: Selling More but Earning Less — Your Investigation
slides.content:
Where to begin: Start with sales transactions and product costs. Calculate revenue, COGS, gross profit and gross margin for each period. Then split the change by product. Check discounts, returns, supplier prices and sales mix. Do not assume the cause until the records support it.

Your turn

A shop’s revenue rises from KSh 500,000 to KSh 650,000. Gross profit falls from KSh 150,000 to KSh 130,000. What is the safest conclusion?

Check your understanding

A shop’s revenue rises from KSh 500,000 to KSh 650,000. Gross profit falls from KSh 150,000 to KSh 130,000. What is the safest conclusion?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

How to report this finding

Gross margin fell from 30% to 20% although revenue rose 30%. The business kept less profit from each shilling of sales. We recommend checking purchase prices, discounts and product mix item by item, and tracking gross margin weekly against an agreed target.

Worked example: Splitting a margin fall by product

A shop had revenue of KSh 300,000 in both months, yet gross profit fell. Split it by product.

  1. Month 1: sugar revenue 100,000, COGS 90,000, gross profit 10,000 (10%). Oil revenue 200,000, COGS 140,000, gross profit 60,000 (30%).
  2. Total gross profit = 10,000 + 60,000 = 70,000. Margin = 70,000 ÷ 300,000 = 23.3%.
  3. Month 2: sugar revenue 200,000, COGS 180,000, gross profit 20,000 (10%). Oil revenue 100,000, COGS 70,000, gross profit 30,000 (30%).
  4. Total gross profit = 20,000 + 30,000 = 50,000. Margin = 50,000 ÷ 300,000 = 16.7%.

Result: neither product's own margin changed (sugar 10%, oil 30%). Customers bought more low-margin sugar and less oil. Meaning: this is a mix effect, so blaming the supplier would be wrong. The product-level records turn a guess into evidence.

Concept checkThe owner says "our supplier raised prices, that is why margin fell". What is the best next step?
Practitioner layer — what to request

Records to request:

  • Sales transactions with date, product, quantity, price and discount
  • Purchase invoices and unit costs by product
  • Returns and credit notes
  • Operating expense ledger
Expert layer

To prove a cause, show it in the records: for a supplier-price claim, show the unit cost rising on invoices; for a discount claim, show discount totals rising. Until then, call it a hypothesis.

Check yourself: How would you word this finding to the shop owner in two sentences?

Answer: Revenue grew but gross profit fell, so the margin is shrinking. We need to check costs, discounts, returns and product mix before changing any prices.

slides.title: Business Problem 2: Money Trapped in Slow-Moving Stock — Understand the Problem
slides.content:
What this means: Inventory is money invested in goods that have not yet been sold. Slow-moving stock can tie up cash, take up storage space and become outdated or expire. Not every slow-moving item is automatically bad: consider seasonality, supplier lead time and expected demand.

Why a business owner should care
Stock is cash sitting on a shelf. A product with a year of stock has been paid for a year before it can pay the business back, and it can still be damaged, stolen, expire or lose its price.

The key measure: Stock cover (months) = Stock on hand ÷ average monthly sales. Stock value = Quantity × unit cost.

Worked example: Stock cover for cement bags

Mary stocks cement. She wants to know whether she holds too much.

  1. Sales in the last 3 months: 80, 70 and 90 bags. Total = 80 + 70 + 90 = 240. Average = 240 ÷ 3 = 80 bags a month.
  2. Stock on hand is 300 bags. Stock cover = 300 ÷ 80 = 3.75 months.
  3. Check stock-outs: none, so the sales history is reliable.
  4. Stock value at cost = 300 × 700 = KSh 210,000.

Result: about 3.75 months of cover, with KSh 210,000 of cash on the shelf. Meaning: the supplier delivers in two weeks (0.5 month), so cover is far longer than the lead time and there is no need to reorder yet. Reorder when cover nears the lead time plus a safety buffer.

Concept checkA product sold only 5 units last month because it was out of stock for three weeks. Its stock cover now looks very high. What should you do?
Practitioner layer — how to spot it

How to spot it in the records:

  1. List each product’s stock on hand and its sales for the last 3 months.
  2. Divide stock by average monthly sales to get stock cover.
  3. Sort from the highest cover down.
  4. Mark items with no sales for 90 days as dead-stock candidates and check them one by one.
Expert layer

Cover uses past sales. A product that was out of stock shows falsely low sales, and a product with a new customer or season may need more than its history suggests. Check stock-out days before judging demand.

Check yourself: What does a stock cover of 12 months mean?

Answer: At the recent selling rate, the stock on hand would take about 12 months to sell, if demand stays stable.

slides.title: Business Problem 2: Money Trapped in Slow-Moving Stock — Worked Example
slides.content:
Follow the numbers slowly. Write down the formula, substitute the values and calculate the result.

Worked example

A store has 120 units of a product. It sells an average of 10 units each month. Stock cover is 120 ÷ 10 = 12 months. This means the current quantity represents about 12 months of sales at the observed rate, assuming demand stays stable.

Interpretation

At the current selling rate this product needs a year to sell. If the supplier delivers in one month, the store can pause reordering for many months without running out. Cover is a signal, not a verdict: first check seasonality and any recent promotion.

Concept checkA product has 60 units and sells 20 a month. The supplier takes 4 months to deliver. What should you do?
Practitioner layer — redo it

Redo the calculation yourself:

  1. Write the formula: stock cover = stock on hand ÷ monthly sales.
  2. Substitute: 120 ÷ 10 = 12 months.
  3. Compare with the supplier lead time (for example 1 month).
  4. Decide: stop reordering, and consider a promotion, until cover falls.
Expert layer

Compare cover with supplier lead time plus a safety buffer. Three months of cover with a one-month lead time is comfortable. Three weeks of cover with a six-week lead time means you should already have reordered.

Check yourself: A product has 90 units and sells 30 a month. The supplier takes 1 month to deliver. What is the cover, and must you reorder today?

Answer: Cover is 3 months. Cover is longer than the 1-month lead time, so there is no urgent reorder; reorder when cover approaches the lead time plus a buffer.

slides.title: Business Problem 2: Money Trapped in Slow-Moving Stock — Your Investigation
slides.content:
Where to begin: Use stock-on-hand records and sales history. Calculate units sold per week or month, stock cover, inventory ageing and stock turnover. Separate seasonal products and items with long supplier lead times. Investigate whether replenishment quantities are too high.

Your turn

A product has 200 units in stock and sells 20 units per month. Approximately how many months of stock does the business hold?

Check your understanding

A product has 200 units in stock and sells 20 units per month. Approximately how many months of stock does the business hold?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

How to report this finding

Product X holds about 12 months of stock, worth KSh __ at cost. We recommend pausing reorders, running a promotion on the excess, and reviewing stock cover for every product monthly.

Worked example: Ranking slow stock by value at cost

A shop lists three slow items and wants to review the most costly first.

  1. Item A: 40 units at cost KSh 250. Value = 40 × 250 = 10,000.
  2. Item B: 15 units at cost KSh 1,200. Value = 15 × 1,200 = 18,000.
  3. Item C: 100 units at cost KSh 50. Value = 100 × 50 = 5,000.
  4. Total = 10,000 + 18,000 + 5,000 = 33,000.
  5. Item B share = 18,000 ÷ 33,000 = 54.5%.

Result: rank B, A, C. Item C has the most units but the least cash tied up. Meaning: start the review with Item B, which holds over half of the KSh 33,000. Use cost, not selling price, because cost shows the cash actually locked up. Also check seasonality and expiry dates before discounting.

Concept checkYou must decide which slow-moving items to review first. How should you rank them?
Practitioner layer — what to request

Records to request:

  • Stock balances at the start and end of the period
  • Sales by product by week or month
  • Purchase orders, supplier lead times and expiry dates
  • Dates when an item was out of stock
Expert layer

Measure trapped money at cost, not at selling price: quantity × unit cost. Rank slow items by cost value so the review starts with the items that lock up the most cash.

Check yourself: Why should you present stock value at cost, not at selling price?

Answer: Cost shows the cash actually tied up. Selling price includes profit the business has not yet earned.

slides.title: Business Problem 3: Rising Costs Eroding Profit — Understand the Problem
slides.content:
What this means: A cost is an amount the business spends. Cost analysis asks which costs are rising, what is driving the change and whether the spending is justified. Always compare like with like: same period length, same categories and consistent accounting treatment.

Why a business owner should care
Costs usually rise a little at a time, so no single bill looks alarming. Without comparing periods, the owner notices only when cash runs short.

The key measure: % change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Expense ratio = Operating expenses ÷ Revenue × 100.

Worked example: Ranking cost increases by shillings

A small office compares expenses for January and February.

  1. Electricity: 10,000 to 12,000. Change = +2,000, which is 2,000 ÷ 10,000 = 20%.
  2. Airtime: 2,000 to 3,000. Change = +1,000, which is 1,000 ÷ 2,000 = 50%.
  3. Transport: 8,000 to 8,800. Change = +800, which is 800 ÷ 8,000 = 10%.
  4. Totals: January 10,000 + 2,000 + 8,000 = 20,000. February 12,000 + 3,000 + 8,800 = 23,800. Change = 3,800, or 3,800 ÷ 20,000 = 19%.

Result: rank by shillings: electricity (+2,000), airtime (+1,000), transport (+800). Meaning: airtime has the largest percentage but electricity explains more of the KSh 3,800 rise. Start there, and check whether any bill was timed unusually.

Concept checkRent (KSh 100,000) rose 5%. Airtime (KSh 4,000) rose 50%. Which should you look at first?
Practitioner layer — how to spot it

How to spot it in the records:

  1. Group expenses into the same categories every month.
  2. Calculate the change in shillings and in percent for each category.
  3. Rank categories by shilling change, not by percent.
  4. Compare with the budget and with the same month last year.
Expert layer

A large percentage on a small cost can matter less than a small percentage on a large cost, so rank by amount first. Also check timing: an annual insurance bill paid this month makes one month look expensive.

Check yourself: Why compare expenses with revenue instead of only with last month?

Answer: Costs that rise with sales are expected. Costs that rise while sales stay flat reduce profit. The expense ratio shows which is happening.

slides.title: Business Problem 3: Rising Costs Eroding Profit — Worked Example
slides.content:
Follow the numbers slowly. Write down the formula, substitute the values and calculate the result.

Worked example

Monthly revenue stays at KSh 1,000,000. Operating expenses rise from KSh 200,000 to KSh 280,000. The increase is KSh 80,000. Percentage increase = 80,000 ÷ 200,000 × 100 = 40%. Expenses now consume 28% of revenue instead of 20%.

Interpretation

Spending rose by 40% while sales did not move, so expenses now take 28 cents of every shilling instead of 20. The next step is to find which categories account for the KSh 80,000, and then which invoices.

Concept checkExpenses were KSh 300,000 on revenue of 1,000,000. Now they are 330,000 on revenue of 1,500,000. What happened to the expense ratio?
Practitioner layer — redo it

Redo the calculation yourself:

  1. Old 200,000, new 280,000. Difference = 80,000.
  2. Percent change = 80,000 ÷ 200,000 = 40%.
  3. Expense ratio before = 200,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 20%.
  4. Expense ratio now = 280,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 28%.
Expert layer

Separate fixed costs (rent) from variable costs (packaging, transport per delivery). Variable costs should move with sales. If they rise faster than sales, look for waste, price increases or errors.

Check yourself: Expenses were 150,000 on revenue of 600,000, and are now 210,000 on revenue of 700,000. Did the expense ratio improve?

Answer: No. It went from 25% (150,000 ÷ 600,000) to 30% (210,000 ÷ 700,000). Expenses grew faster than sales.

slides.title: Business Problem 3: Rising Costs Eroding Profit — Your Investigation
slides.content:
Where to begin: Obtain the expense ledger, supplier invoices and budget. Group expenses into consistent categories. Compare the current period with the previous period and budget. Drill into the categories responsible for the difference, then inspect transactions and supplier or usage changes.

Your turn

Revenue stays at KSh 1,000,000 while operating expenses rise from KSh 200,000 to KSh 280,000. What is the expense increase?

Check your understanding

Revenue stays at KSh 1,000,000 while operating expenses rise from KSh 200,000 to KSh 280,000. What is the expense increase?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

How to report this finding

Operating expenses rose 40% (KSh 80,000) while revenue stayed flat. Expenses now take 28% of revenue instead of 20%. The increase is mostly in __. We recommend reviewing __ and monitoring the expense ratio monthly.

Worked example: Price or quantity behind a cost rise

A bakery's packaging cost rose. Separate price from quantity.

  1. January: 500 boxes at KSh 20 = 10,000.
  2. February: 600 boxes at KSh 25 = 15,000.
  3. Total increase = 15,000 − 10,000 = 5,000.
  4. Price effect = (25 − 20) × 600 = 3,000.
  5. Quantity effect = (600 − 500) × 20 = 2,000.
  6. Check: 3,000 + 2,000 = 5,000.

Result: KSh 3,000 of the rise comes from the higher box price and KSh 2,000 from using more boxes. Meaning: boxes used rose 20% (100 ÷ 500), which may simply follow more orders, so the larger issue is price. Ask the supplier for the price list and invoices before negotiating.

Concept checkDelivery costs rose from KSh 10,000 to 15,000 while deliveries rose from 50 to 100. What does this show?
Practitioner layer — what to request

Records to request:

  • Expense ledger by transaction
  • Supplier invoices and price lists
  • Budget for the period
  • Bank or mobile-money statements to confirm payments
Expert layer

Separate price from quantity. Did the business pay more per unit, or use more units? The first points to supplier negotiation. The second points to controlling usage.

Check yourself: Why list the biggest shilling increases first in your report?

Answer: They explain most of the problem. Starting there saves time and keeps management’s attention on what matters.

slides.title: Business Problem 4: Hidden or Uncontrolled Expenses — Understand the Problem
slides.content:
What this means: Small expenses can become significant when they occur frequently. Poorly described transactions, duplicate entries and inconsistent categories make spending difficult to understand. An unusual transaction is a reason to investigate, not proof of wrongdoing.

Why a business owner should care
Small, frequent spends such as airtime, transport and “miscellaneous” escape attention. A poor record also makes it impossible to tell real costs from mistakes or misuse.

The key measure: Category share % = Category spending ÷ Total spending × 100.

Concept checkThe ledger shows two payments of KSh 5,000 to the same payee on the same date. What is the sensible first step?
Practitioner layer — how to spot it

How to spot it in the records:

  1. Standardise category names (for example “Transpot” and “Transport” are one category).
  2. Look for duplicates: same date, same amount, same payee.
  3. Flag vague descriptions such as “misc” and round-number payments.
  4. Check each flagged item against a receipt or approval.
Expert layer

An unusual entry is a reason to ask, not an accusation. Report it neutrally (“could not be matched to a receipt”) and let the owner decide. Never accuse a person from data alone.

Check yourself: What is a sensible first check on a possible duplicate payment?

Answer: Compare the date, amount and payee and look at the receipt or invoice. Two identical payments may be genuine.

slides.title: Business Problem 4: Hidden or Uncontrolled Expenses — Worked Example
slides.content:
Follow the numbers slowly. Write down the formula, substitute the values and calculate the result.

Worked example

Suppose transport costs are KSh 18,000, airtime is KSh 7,000 and repairs are KSh 25,000. Combined spending is KSh 50,000. Transport is 36% of the total, airtime 14% and repairs 50%. Compare the total and each category with the previous month, the budget and supporting documents.

Interpretation

Repairs are half of this spending, so that is the first place to ask questions: what was repaired, who approved it and where are the receipts? A high share does not mean wrongdoing. It tells you where to look first.

Concept checkThe expense ledger lists both "Transpot" and "Transport" as categories. Why does this matter?
Practitioner layer — redo it

Redo the calculation yourself:

  1. Add the categories: 18,000 + 7,000 + 25,000 = 50,000.
  2. Repairs share = 25,000 ÷ 50,000 = 50%.
  3. Transport share = 18,000 ÷ 50,000 = 36%.
  4. Airtime share = 7,000 ÷ 50,000 = 14%.
Expert layer

Usually a few categories make up most of the spending. Sort categories from largest to smallest and find the ones that make up about 80% of the total. Start the review there.

Check yourself: Transport 18,000, airtime 7,000, repairs 25,000. What percentage of the total is repairs?

Answer: 50% (25,000 ÷ 50,000).

slides.title: Business Problem 4: Hidden or Uncontrolled Expenses — Your Investigation
slides.content:
Where to begin: Request the transaction-level expense ledger. Standardise category names, check duplicates, review dates and amounts, and compare actual spending with budget. Trace unusual entries to receipts, approvals or invoices. Record unresolved items rather than guessing.

Your turn

Why should an analyst examine expenses by category instead of looking only at the total?

Check your understanding

Why should an analyst examine expenses by category instead of looking only at the total?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

How to report this finding

Repairs account for 50% of this month’s spending. __ of the __ repair entries have no receipt (KSh __). We recommend requiring a receipt and an approval for payments above KSh __.

Worked example: Reading a month's expense ledger

A transaction-level ledger for one month totals KSh 80,000.

  1. Repairs 32,000, transport 24,000, airtime 16,000, miscellaneous 8,000. Check: 32,000 + 24,000 + 16,000 + 8,000 = 80,000.
  2. Repairs share = 32,000 ÷ 80,000 = 40%. Transport = 30%. Airtime = 20%. Miscellaneous = 10%.
  3. Repairs and transport together = 40% + 30% = 70%, so start there.
  4. Two payments of KSh 4,500 to the same garage on the same date are flagged. As a share of repairs: 4,500 ÷ 32,000 = 14.1%.

Result: repairs are the largest category, and one possible duplicate is worth checking. Meaning: compare both payments with receipts. If only one has a receipt, report "one payment could not be matched", not an accusation.

Concept checkTotal expenses were KSh 80,000 in both months. Why still examine them by category?
Practitioner layer — what to request

Records to request:

  • Transaction-level expense ledger with date, payee and description
  • Receipts, invoices and approvals
  • Budget by category
  • Bank or mobile-money statements
Expert layer

With thousands of entries, check every large item and a random sample of the small ones. Report the sample size so the reader knows how far to trust the finding.

Check yourself: Why is “could not be matched to a receipt” better wording than “someone stole money”?

Answer: It states what the evidence shows. A missing receipt can have many innocent explanations.

slides.title: Business Problem 5: Missed Growth Opportunities — Understand the Problem
slides.content:
What this means: Growth analysis looks for places where a business could serve more customers, sell more effectively or improve its offer. A low-performing branch or product is a signal to investigate, not automatic proof of poor management.

Why a business owner should care
Growth is often hidden in what the business is not doing: customers asking for items it does not stock, a branch open fewer days, or a busy hour with one cashier.

The key measure: Revenue per trading day = Revenue ÷ days open. Share of total % = Branch revenue ÷ total revenue × 100. Conversion rate % = Buyers ÷ visitors × 100.

Worked example: Comparing two branches fairly

Branch X earned KSh 180,000 in 20 days open. Branch Y earned KSh 240,000 in 30 days open.

  1. Total revenue = 180,000 + 240,000 = 420,000.
  2. Share of total: X = 180,000 ÷ 420,000 = 42.9%. Y = 240,000 ÷ 420,000 = 57.1%.
  3. Revenue per trading day: X = 180,000 ÷ 20 = 9,000.
  4. Y = 240,000 ÷ 30 = 8,000.

Result: Y has the larger share, but X earns KSh 1,000 more for every day it is open. Meaning: X is not the weaker branch. It trades fewer days. Before any conclusion, also compare profit, costs and local demand, and look at several months, not one.

Concept checkBranch A was open 20 days and Branch B 30 days. What is the fairest way to compare their sales?
Practitioner layer — how to spot it

How to spot it in the records:

  1. Split results by branch, product, customer type and time.
  2. Compare revenue per day open, and profit, not only total revenue.
  3. Count stock-outs and lost-sale requests.
  4. List the products customers ask for that the business does not sell.
Expert layer

Do not mistake correlation for cause. A branch in a quiet area may never match the others. Benchmark against comparable locations and look at several months, not one.

Check yourself: Why compare profit, not only revenue, between branches?

Answer: A branch with lower revenue may have lower costs and more profit. Revenue alone hides this.

slides.title: Business Problem 5: Missed Growth Opportunities — Worked Example
slides.content:
Follow the numbers slowly. Write down the formula, substitute the values and calculate the result.

Worked example

Three branches report monthly revenue of KSh 100,000, KSh 150,000 and KSh 250,000. The total is KSh 500,000, so the lowest branch, Branch A, earns 20% of revenue. Before recommending action, compare customer traffic, operating days, product availability, conversion rate, branch size and local demand.

Interpretation

Branch A earns 20% of revenue, but that alone does not make it weak. A smaller branch with low costs can earn more profit than a larger one. Compare revenue per trading day, costs and profit before drawing a conclusion.

Concept checkBranch X earned KSh 180,000 in 20 days open. Branch Y earned KSh 240,000 in 30 days open. Which performs better per trading day?
Practitioner layer — redo it

Redo the calculation yourself:

  1. Branch A: 100,000 over 20 days open = 5,000 per day.
  2. Branch B: 150,000 over 30 days open = 5,000 per day.
  3. Per day, the two branches perform equally.
  4. The revenue gap comes from trading days, not from performance.
Expert layer

Test, do not assume. Run a small pilot (for example, extend opening hours for 4 weeks or stock a requested item) with a defined measure and a comparison period. Then decide.

Check yourself: Branch A earns 100,000 in 20 days open. Branch B earns 150,000 in 30 days open. Which performs better per trading day?

Answer: Neither. Both earn KSh 5,000 per trading day. The difference is the number of days open.

slides.title: Business Problem 5: Missed Growth Opportunities — Your Investigation
slides.content:
Where to begin: Segment results by branch, product, customer type and time period. Compare revenue and profit, not revenue alone. Look for unmet demand, frequent stock-outs, low conversion or products customers request but cannot buy. Test a specific action and measure the result.

Your turn

Branch A has the lowest revenue. What should the analyst do next?

Check your understanding

Branch A has the lowest revenue. What should the analyst do next?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

How to report this finding

Branch A earns 20% of revenue but traded 20 of 30 days. Per trading day it performs the same as Branch B. We recommend a 4-week pilot of longer opening days at Branch A and tracking daily sales.

Worked example: Testing a longer-opening pilot

A branch opens 20 days in a 4-week period. You propose opening 28 days for the next 4 weeks.

  1. Baseline: sales KSh 100,000 in 20 days, which is 5,000 a day.
  2. Pilot result: KSh 154,000 in 28 days, which is 5,500 a day.
  3. Extra revenue = 154,000 − 100,000 = 54,000.
  4. At a 30% gross margin, extra gross profit = 54,000 × 30% = 16,200.
  5. Extra wages and power cost KSh 12,000.
  6. Net gain = 16,200 − 12,000 = 4,200.

Result: the pilot gained KSh 4,200 over the baseline. Meaning: it paid for itself, but this is one period. Repeat it, or extend the pilot, before committing permanently. The pilot limited the risk and gave evidence.

Concept checkYou think longer opening days could lift a branch's sales. What is the best recommendation?
Practitioner layer — what to request

Records to request:

  • Sales by branch and by day
  • Opening days and hours
  • Customer counts (footfall) if recorded
  • Stock-out lists, customer requests and branch costs
Expert layer

Beware small samples. One bad week at a branch is not a trend. State how many periods you examined so the reader can judge how firm the finding is.

Check yourself: Why should a recommendation include a pilot with a measure?

Answer: A pilot limits the risk and gives evidence. Management can see whether the action worked before committing more money.

slides.title: Business Problem 6: Unprofitable Customers — Understand the Problem
slides.content:
What this means: A customer who spends a lot is not always the most profitable. Discounts, delivery, returns, support time, credit losses and servicing costs can reduce the value of a customer relationship.

Why a business owner should care
The biggest customer by sales may demand deep discounts, free delivery, frequent returns and late payment. Knowing profit by customer shows who to protect and whom to re-price.

The key measure: Customer gross profit = Revenue × gross margin %. Profit after servicing = Gross profit − costs caused by that customer (delivery, returns, credit losses).

Concept checkA customer buys KSh 500,000 at a 5% gross margin and costs KSh 30,000 in delivery and credit follow-up. What is the position?
Practitioner layer — how to spot it

How to spot it in the records:

  1. Link every sale to a customer ID.
  2. Calculate revenue, discounts, returns and gross profit for each customer.
  3. Add servicing costs where they are recorded.
  4. Rank customers by profit, not by revenue.
Expert layer

Sharing costs between customers involves judgement. State the rule you used (for example delivery cost by number of trips). Also protect privacy: show named-customer results only to people allowed to see them.

Check yourself: Can the largest customer by sales be the least profitable?

Answer: Yes. Discounts, returns and servicing costs can outweigh the gross profit.

slides.title: Business Problem 6: Unprofitable Customers — Worked Example
slides.content:
Follow the numbers slowly. Write down the formula, substitute the values and calculate the result.

Worked example

Customer A buys KSh 100,000 at a 10% gross margin: KSh 10,000 gross profit. Customer B buys KSh 70,000 at a 25% gross margin: KSh 17,500 gross profit. Customer B generates less revenue but more gross profit before customer-specific servicing costs.

Interpretation

If serving Customer A also costs KSh 12,000 in delivery and credit follow-up, A’s profit after servicing is 10,000 − 12,000 = −KSh 2,000. Customer B would still show KSh 17,500 before its own servicing costs. Revenue ranks A first; profit ranks B first.

Concept checkCustomer P buys KSh 100,000 at 20% margin. Customer Q buys KSh 150,000 at 10% margin. Who gives more gross profit?
Practitioner layer — redo it

Redo the calculation yourself:

  1. Customer A: 100,000 × 10% = 10,000.
  2. Customer B: 70,000 × 25% = 17,500.
  3. Rank by gross profit: B first, A second.
  4. Subtract servicing costs for each customer before final conclusions.
Expert layer

Look at the trend and payment behaviour too. A new customer with low profit this quarter may become valuable. An old customer with falling orders and late payments is a risk.

Check yourself: Customer C buys 200,000 at 8% margin. Customer D buys 90,000 at 20% margin. Who gives more gross profit?

Answer: Customer D: 90,000 × 20% = 18,000, against 200,000 × 8% = 16,000 for Customer C.

slides.title: Business Problem 6: Unprofitable Customers — Your Investigation
slides.content:
Where to begin: Connect sales to customer IDs. Calculate revenue, discounts, returns and gross profit by customer. If possible, include delivery, support and collection costs. Check customer privacy and access permissions. Use a suitable period and avoid treating one unusual order as a long-term pattern.

Your turn

Customer A generates KSh 100,000 revenue at 10% margin. Customer B generates KSh 70,000 at 25% margin. Who generates more gross profit before servicing costs?

Check your understanding

Customer A generates KSh 100,000 revenue at 10% margin. Customer B generates KSh 70,000 at 25% margin. Who generates more gross profit before servicing costs?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

How to report this finding

Customer A is our largest by sales but earns only KSh 10,000 gross profit, which is less than the KSh 12,000 it costs to serve. We recommend a minimum order and a delivery charge, and reviewing the result in three months.

Worked example: Profit after servicing two customers

Customer P is the largest buyer. Customer Q is smaller. Compare their profit.

  1. P: revenue 300,000 at 12% margin. Gross profit = 300,000 × 12% = 36,000.
  2. P servicing: delivery 15,000 + credit follow-up 6,000 = 21,000.
  3. P profit after servicing = 36,000 − 21,000 = 15,000.
  4. Q: revenue 150,000 at 30% margin. Gross profit = 150,000 × 30% = 45,000.
  5. Q servicing = 5,000. Profit after servicing = 45,000 − 5,000 = 40,000.

Result: by revenue P ranks first. By profit after servicing Q ranks first, with 40,000 against 15,000. Meaning: protect Q. For P, discuss re-pricing, a minimum order or a delivery charge with the owner. The cost-sharing rule used (actual delivery trips) should be stated in the report.

Concept checkA customer shows a loss after servicing costs. What should the analyst suggest first?
Practitioner layer — what to request

Records to request:

  • Sales with customer ID
  • Discount records and returns
  • Delivery and credit costs by customer
  • Payment dates, to measure days to pay
Expert layer

Do not drop a customer because of a spreadsheet. Options include re-pricing, a minimum order, a delivery charge or tighter credit terms. Discuss them with the business owner before acting.

Check yourself: Why list the servicing costs separately from gross profit?

Answer: They show how much of the profit is lost to serving the customer, and they let management see which cost to change.

slides.title: Business Problem 7: Unclear Business Performance — Understand the Problem
slides.content:
What this means: A business cannot manage performance consistently if it has no agreed measures, targets or reporting periods. A useful KPI has a clear definition, a reliable source, an owner and a reason for being monitored.

Why a business owner should care
Without agreed targets, every month’s result can be explained away. A small set of defined KPIs shows whether the business is on track and who must act.

The key measure: Target achievement % = Actual ÷ Target × 100. Variance = Actual − Target.

Worked example: Actual versus target for three KPIs

A shop manager agrees three KPIs with the owner for June.

  1. Sales: target 600,000, actual 570,000. Achievement = 570,000 ÷ 600,000 × 100 = 95%. Variance = 570,000 − 600,000 = −30,000.
  2. Gross margin: target 30%, actual 27%. Variance = 27 − 30 = −3 percentage points.
  3. Expense ratio: target 20%, actual 22%. Variance = 22 − 20 = +2 percentage points.

Result: sales are 5% short, margin is 3 points low and the expense ratio is 2 points high. Meaning: for the expense ratio, above target is bad, so a positive variance is a warning. All three miss. Each KPI needs an owner, and last three months' trend should sit beside each result before anyone is asked to act.

Concept checkWhich of these is the best-defined KPI?
Practitioner layer — how to spot it

How to spot it in the records:

  1. Choose 4 to 6 KPIs linked to goals, such as sales, gross margin, expense ratio, stock cover and cash.
  2. Write each KPI’s definition, source and owner.
  3. Show actual versus target, plus the last three periods.
  4. Use colours only for thresholds that management has agreed.
Expert layer

Targets must be realistic and based on history. An unreachable target discourages staff and a weak one hides problems. Beware of gaming: if staff are rewarded only for sales, they may cut margin to hit the number.

Check yourself: What makes a KPI useful?

Answer: A clear definition, a reliable data source, an owner and a target linked to a business goal.

slides.title: Business Problem 7: Unclear Business Performance — Worked Example
slides.content:
Follow the numbers slowly. Write down the formula, substitute the values and calculate the result.

Worked example

Monthly sales target is KSh 800,000. Actual sales are KSh 680,000. Target achievement = 680,000 ÷ 800,000 × 100 = 85%. The shortfall is KSh 120,000. This tells management the size of the gap; it does not yet explain the cause.

Interpretation

Sales reached 85% of target, KSh 120,000 short. Management now knows how big the gap is. The next question is where it came from: which products, branches or weeks. Ask this before anyone is blamed.

Concept checkSales reached 85% of target this month. The previous two months were 70% and 78%. What does the trend say?
Practitioner layer — redo it

Redo the calculation yourself:

  1. Write the formula: achievement = actual ÷ target × 100.
  2. Substitute: 680,000 ÷ 800,000 = 0.85, which is 85%.
  3. Variance = 680,000 − 800,000 = −120,000.
  4. Add context: was last month better or worse?
Expert layer

Always add a trend. Reaching 85% after 95% and 90% shows deterioration. Reaching 85% after 70% and 78% shows improvement. One number rarely tells the story.

Check yourself: Target 500,000 and actual 550,000. What are the target achievement and the variance?

Answer: 110% achievement and a variance of +KSh 50,000.

slides.title: Business Problem 7: Unclear Business Performance — Your Investigation
slides.content:
Where to begin: Agree on a small set of KPIs linked to business objectives. Define each calculation, reporting frequency, target and data source. Show actual versus target and the trend. Add context so a manager can understand what needs attention.

Your turn

A business targets KSh 800,000 and achieves KSh 680,000. What is target achievement?

Check your understanding

A business targets KSh 800,000 and achieves KSh 680,000. What is target achievement?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

How to report this finding

Sales reached 85% of the KSh 800,000 target, a shortfall of KSh 120,000. This is down from __% last month. We will break the gap down by product and branch and report back next week.

Worked example: Reading a trend against target

A shop's monthly sales target is KSh 500,000. Results for three months:

  1. January: 450,000. Achievement = 450,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 90%. Variance = 450,000 − 500,000 = −50,000.
  2. February: 425,000. Achievement = 425,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 85%. Variance = −75,000.
  3. March: 400,000. Achievement = 400,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 80%. Variance = −100,000.

Result: 90%, 85%, then 80%. The gap grows by KSh 25,000 each month. Meaning: March alone says "80% of target", but the trend shows steady deterioration. Report both. Management should ask where the gap comes from (product, branch or week) before anyone is blamed, and a named KPI owner should explain it.

Concept checkSales staff are rewarded only for reaching the sales target. What risk should you point out?
Practitioner layer — what to request

Records to request:

  • Written targets for the period
  • Actual results from the source system
  • KPI definitions and the reporting calendar
  • A list of KPI owners
Expert layer

Keep a KPI dictionary with name, formula, source, frequency and owner. Most arguments about numbers are really arguments about definitions.

Check yourself: Why should every KPI have an owner?

Answer: Someone must be responsible for explaining the number and acting on it. Without an owner, nobody acts.

slides.title: Business Problem 8: Decisions Without Reliable Data — Understand the Problem
slides.content:
What this means: A dashboard is only as trustworthy as the records and calculations behind it. Data quality includes accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity and timeliness. When totals disagree, pause and reconcile before presenting conclusions.

Why a business owner should care
A wrong number presented with confidence is worse than no number, because people act on it. Trust is built by showing that the totals reconcile.

The key measure: Difference = Reported total − Source total. Difference % = Difference ÷ Source total × 100.

Worked example: Reconciling a dashboard to the source

A dashboard shows KSh 840,000 in sales. The source file totals KSh 800,000.

  1. Difference = 840,000 − 800,000 = 40,000.
  2. Difference % = 40,000 ÷ 800,000 × 100 = 5%.
  3. Count rows: source 400, dashboard 410. Ten extra rows.
  4. Check for repeated IDs: 10 transactions appear twice, each KSh 4,000. 10 × 4,000 = 40,000.
  5. Remove the duplicates in the calculation: 840,000 − 40,000 = 800,000.

Result: the dashboard was 5% too high because ten transactions were counted twice, and now both totals agree at KSh 800,000. Meaning: fix the calculation, not the source. Agreement shows the two match, not that the data is right, so also run reasonableness checks.

Concept checkA dashboard total and the bank total are both KSh 2,000,000. Does this prove the data is correct?
Practitioner layer — how to spot it

How to spot it in the records:

  1. Count rows in the source and in the report.
  2. Check for duplicates (the same ID twice) and blank values.
  3. Compare the date range and filters used.
  4. Reconcile to a trusted total, such as accounting or bank records.
Expert layer

Reconciling does not prove the data is right, only that two sources agree. If both contain the same error, they will agree. Add reasonableness checks: negative quantities, future dates, prices 100 times the normal.

Check yourself: What is the first step when a dashboard total and the source total disagree?

Answer: Pause and find the cause of the difference. Do not present the dashboard and do not alter the source to match.

slides.title: Business Problem 8: Decisions Without Reliable Data — Worked Example
slides.content:
Follow the numbers slowly. Write down the formula, substitute the values and calculate the result.

Worked example

A dashboard reports KSh 500,000 in sales, but the source transactions total KSh 450,000. The difference is KSh 50,000, which is 11.1% of the source total. Check date filters, duplicate records, missing transactions, returns, discounts, cancelled orders and calculation rules. Do not simply adjust the source to match the dashboard.

Interpretation

The dashboard is 11.1% higher than the source. Find the cause before presenting: duplicated rows, cancelled orders counted, a wrong date range, or returns not subtracted. Correct the calculation. Change source data only if you can prove the source itself is wrong.

Concept checkA dashboard shows KSh 600,000 and the source totals KSh 540,000. What is the difference as a percentage of the source?
Practitioner layer — redo it

Redo the calculation yourself:

  1. Dashboard total 1,200,000; source total 1,050,000.
  2. Difference = 1,200,000 − 1,050,000 = 150,000.
  3. Difference % = 150,000 ÷ 1,050,000 = 14.3%.
  4. List possible causes and check them one at a time.
Expert layer

Keep a short change log: what you changed and why. If you remove duplicates, say how many and by which rule. A reviewer should be able to reproduce your numbers.

Check yourself: A dashboard shows 1,200,000 and the source totals 1,050,000. What is the difference and what is it as a percentage of the source?

Answer: KSh 150,000, which is 14.3% of the source. Check duplicates, date filters and cancelled orders.

slides.title: Business Problem 8: Decisions Without Reliable Data — Your Investigation
slides.content:
Where to begin: Document the source of each field and KPI. Check row counts, missing values, duplicates, valid dates and numeric ranges. Reconcile totals against a trusted report or accounting record. Record any unresolved limitation in the final presentation.

Your turn

A dashboard total disagrees with the source transactions. What should you do first?

Check your understanding

A dashboard total disagrees with the source transactions. What should you do first?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

How to report this finding

The dashboard showed KSh 500,000 but the source records total KSh 450,000. The KSh 50,000 gap came from __. After the correction the figures agree. Remaining limitation: __.

Worked example: Cleaning an export with a change log

You receive a raw sales export. Keep it unchanged and work on a copy.

  1. Raw export: 1,000 rows totalling KSh 2,000,000.
  2. Duplicate check: 20 rows repeat an existing transaction ID, each KSh 2,500. 20 × 2,500 = 50,000.
  3. Remove them in a documented Power Query step: 1,000 − 20 = 980 rows. Total = 2,000,000 − 50,000 = 1,950,000.
  4. Reconcile to the accounting total of KSh 1,950,000. Difference = 1,950,000 − 1,950,000 = 0.
  5. Reasonableness: 2 rows have negative quantities. They look like returns, so keep them and note them.

Result: the cleaned data matches accounting. Meaning: the change log (20 duplicates removed by ID, 2 negatives kept and flagged) lets a reviewer reproduce every number.

Concept checkYou find duplicate rows in a sales export. What is the best way to correct them?
Practitioner layer — what to request

Records to request:

  • The raw source export, kept unchanged
  • The dashboard’s measure definitions
  • A trusted accounting or bank total
  • A data dictionary describing each field
Expert layer

Validate first, analyse second. Keep the raw data untouched and make all corrections in documented, repeatable steps such as Power Query or a script, so the work can be re-run and checked.

Check yourself: Why keep the raw data unchanged?

Answer: It lets you and others re-run and check every correction. If you edit the original you cannot prove what changed.

slides.title: From Business Question to Data: What Should You Request?
slides.content:
Do not ask a business for “all the data” without a reason. Request only what is relevant to the question, and agree on a suitable date range.

QuestionUseful records
Are we making profit?Sales, purchase costs, returns and expenses
Is stock moving?Stock balances, stock movements and sales history
Which customers are valuable?Customer IDs, sales, discounts, returns and service costs
Why did costs rise?Expense ledger, budgets, invoices and supplier records
Are we meeting targets?KPI definitions, targets and actual results

Important: Protect confidential business and customer information. Request appropriate access, use only what is necessary and follow the organisation’s data-handling rules.

Worked example: Turning a question into a data request

A hardware shop owner asks: "Which customers are valuable?"

  1. Write the question in one sentence: which customers give the most profit over the last 6 months?
  2. List only the records that answer it: sales with customer ID, discounts, returns and delivery costs.
  3. Leave out what is not needed: phone numbers, staff records and personal details.
  4. Agree the date range (January to June) and file format (Excel).
  5. Check size: 6 months × about 2,000 rows a month = 12,000 rows, well under Excel's limit of about 1,000,000.
  6. Ask who owns each record and who may see the results.

Result: a short, justified request. Meaning: asking for the minimum data speeds up the work, lowers the privacy risk and keeps the analysis focused on the question.

Concept checkA pharmacy owner asks "Which customers are valuable?". Which data request is best?
Practitioner layer
  1. Write the business question in one sentence.
  2. List only the records that answer it.
  3. Agree the date range and the file format.
  4. Ask who owns each record and who may see it.
Expert layer

Ask for the minimum data that answers the question. Extra personal or confidential data increases risk and slows you down. Agree in writing what you will keep, for how long and who may see the results.

Check yourself: Which records would you request for the question “Is stock moving?”

Answer: Stock balances, stock movements and sales history for the same period.

slides.title: Choose the Right Tool for the Job
slides.content:
You do not need to use every tool in every project. Choose based on the size of the data, the task and the skills available.

  • Excel: inspect files, reconcile totals, use formulas, PivotTables and quick analysis.
  • Power Query: repeat data-cleaning and combining steps consistently.
  • SQL: retrieve, filter, join and summarise records stored in relational databases.
  • Power BI: create a reusable data model, measures and interactive management reports.
  • Python with pandas: automate repeatable analysis, investigate larger datasets and perform specialised calculations.

Practical rule: understand the business question and validate the data before choosing a tool. A complicated tool cannot repair an unclear question.

Worked example: Choosing a tool for three tasks

An analyst at a distributor has three tasks. Apply the practical rule.

  1. Task 1: a monthly sales file of 12,000 rows arrives with the same messy layout each month. 12,000 is far below about 1,000,000, so Excel can hold it. Because the same cleaning repeats, use Power Query.
  2. Task 2: a database holds 4,000,000 sales rows but only November by branch is needed. This exceeds Excel's limit, so use SQL to filter and summarise.
  3. Task 3: branch managers want to explore results themselves. Build a Power BI model after the data is validated.

Result: three tasks, three tools. Meaning: choose the simplest reliable, repeatable tool. In every case, define the question and validate the data first, because a complicated tool cannot repair an unclear question.

Concept checkA database holds 4 million sales rows. You need only November sales by branch. Which tool should you use first?
Practitioner layer
  1. Is the data small enough for Excel (about one million rows at most)? If yes, start there.
  2. Must the same cleaning be repeated every month? Use Power Query.
  3. Is the data in a database? Use SQL to extract only what you need.
  4. Must managers explore results themselves? Build a Power BI model.
Expert layer

Choose the simplest tool that is reliable and repeatable. Skill is not shown by using the most complex tool. Python is valuable for automation and larger or more specialised analysis, but a clear question and validated data matter more.

Check yourself: A monthly report must refresh with new files each month without redoing the cleaning. Which tool helps most?

Answer: Power Query (in Excel or Power BI), because its recorded cleaning steps can be refreshed with new data.

slides.title: How to Present a Finding So Management Understands
slides.content:
Use this simple five-part structure when presenting an important finding.

  1. Finding: State what the analysis shows.
  2. Evidence: Give the measure, period and comparison.
  3. Meaning: Explain why it matters to the business.
  4. Action: Recommend a practical next step.
  5. Measure: Explain how management will know whether the action worked.
Example:

“Gross margin fell from 30% to 20% between January and February, even though revenue increased. This means the business retained less gross profit from each shilling of sales. We recommend reviewing purchase prices, discounting and product mix by item. Management should monitor gross margin weekly and compare it with the agreed target.”

Do not claim that a supplier caused the decline until the supplier and purchase records confirm it.

Concept checkWhich statement best follows the five-part structure for presenting a finding?
Practitioner layer
  1. Write your finding as one sentence with a number.
  2. Add the evidence: measure, period and comparison.
  3. Say why it matters and recommend one action.
  4. Name the measure that will show if the action worked.
Expert layer

Lead with the finding, not the method. Managers often read only the first two lines. Put limitations in plain words straight after the finding so nobody is surprised later.

Check yourself: Rewrite “Gross profit is 20%” as a finding a manager can use.

Answer: For example: “Gross margin fell from 30% to 20% between January and February. We recommend reviewing purchase prices and discounts by product.”

slides.title: Capstone: Investigate a Retail Business
slides.content:
Your assignment: A retail owner says: “We sell every day, but there is never enough money. Some products move quickly, others stay on the shelves, and I cannot tell which products actually make us money.”

Your job is to conduct a structured investigation. You are not expected to know the answer before examining the records.

  1. Clarify what the owner means by “not enough money”. Is it low profit, late customer payments, high expenses or cash tied up in stock?
  2. Request sales, purchase-cost, returns, expense and inventory records for an agreed period.
  3. Validate the records and reconcile important totals.
  4. Calculate revenue, gross profit, gross margin and operating expenses.
  5. Identify profitable products and slow-moving stock.
  6. Investigate expense changes and customer profitability where the data permits.
  7. Build a concise dashboard with definitions, targets and trends.
  8. Write recommendations with evidence, owners and follow-up measures.

Worked example: Why a profitable shop has no cash

The owner says: "We sell every day, but there is never enough money." After clarifying and validating, you calculate (simplified).

  1. Revenue 900,000, COGS 630,000. Gross profit = 900,000 − 630,000 = 270,000. Margin = 270,000 ÷ 900,000 = 30%.
  2. Operating expenses 210,000. Net profit = 270,000 − 210,000 = 60,000.
  3. Customers still owe 40,000. That is profit on paper, not cash received.
  4. Extra stock of 100,000 was bought and is still on the shelves.
  5. Cash change = 60,000 − 40,000 − 100,000 = −80,000.

Result: a profit of KSh 60,000 but cash down by about KSh 80,000. Meaning: the problem is cash tied up in stock and unpaid sales, not low profit. State that this uses three months of data, then investigate stock cover and credit.

Concept checkThe owner of a retail business gives you only three months of records. What should you do?
Practitioner layer
  1. Spend the first session on the question, the definitions and the data request.
  2. Validate and reconcile before any chart.
  3. Calculate the main measures and compare periods.
  4. Write findings and recommendations using the five-part structure.
Expert layer

Professionals state their assumptions. If the owner gives you only three months of data, say so and limit your conclusions. A well-scoped, honest piece of work earns more trust than an over-confident one.

Check yourself: What should you do first in the capstone, before opening any tool?

Answer: Clarify what the owner means by “not enough money” and agree the definitions and the records you need.

slides.title: Capstone: Your Final Consultant Checklist
slides.content:
Before you present, check that you can answer each question clearly.

  • Can I explain the business question in one sentence?
  • Can I identify where every important number came from?
  • Have I checked missing values, duplicates and inconsistent records?
  • Are my calculations correct and clearly defined?
  • Have I compared equivalent periods and segments?
  • Can I distinguish a proven finding from a possible explanation?
  • Does every recommendation connect to evidence?
  • Have I explained limitations and risks?
  • Can management understand what action to take next?
  • Have I defined how results will be monitored?

Worked example: Checking equivalent periods

Checklist item: "Have I compared equivalent periods?" A draft says sales fell from January to February.

  1. January sales: KSh 310,000 over 31 days. February: KSh 280,000 over 28 days.
  2. Raw change = 280,000 − 310,000 = −30,000, and −30,000 ÷ 310,000 = −9.7%.
  3. January per day = 310,000 ÷ 31 = 10,000.
  4. February per day = 280,000 ÷ 28 = 10,000.

Result: daily sales are identical at KSh 10,000. Meaning: the draft's "9.7% fall" only reflects three fewer days. Without this check the report would send management chasing a problem that does not exist. Correct the finding and state the comparison used, so a sceptical owner asking "how do you know?" gets a clear answer.

Concept checkYour records show margin fell, but you have not checked discounts. Which wording is best?
Practitioner layer
  1. Work through the checklist with a partner who is not on the project.
  2. Mark each answer Yes, No or Partly, and fix every No.
  3. Re-check the three most important numbers against the source.
Expert layer

Before you present, play the sceptical owner. Ask: “How do you know?”, “What would change your mind?” and “What if the data is wrong?”. If you cannot answer, do more work or state the limitation.

Check yourself: What is the difference between a proven finding and a possible explanation?

Answer: A proven finding is supported by the records. A possible explanation is a hypothesis that still needs checking.

slides.title: Final Assessment: Think Before You Recommend
slides.content:
Use this final scenario to test your judgement.

Check your understanding

A business has rising revenue, falling gross margin and increasing stock levels. What is the best first response?

Choose one answer. If it is incorrect, read the explanation and try again.

Professional analysts do not rush to sound certain. They become trusted by being accurate, clear about evidence and practical about next steps.

Concept checkRevenue is rising, margin is falling and stock is increasing. Which statement is the safest?
Practitioner layer
  1. Read the scenario and say in your own words what is known and unknown.
  2. Remove answers that jump to a conclusion or a drastic action.
  3. Choose the answer that investigates the evidence first.
Expert layer

The best answer is usually the one that gathers evidence before acting. Rising revenue with falling margin and rising stock suggests several possible causes at once, such as discounting, rising costs or over-buying, and each needs checking.

Check yourself: Why is “stop buying every product” a poor first response?

Answer: It is drastic and not based on evidence. Some products may be profitable and fast-moving. Investigate first.

slides.title: Where to Go Next: Turn Learning into Practice
slides.content:
You have completed the learning material when you can explain the eight business problems, calculate the basic measures, identify the records needed and communicate a defensible recommendation.

Your next practical step: Take a small, non-confidential retail dataset and repeat the capstone process. Begin in Excel, validate your totals, then use Power Query, SQL or Power BI where appropriate. Keep a short record of the question, method, findings, limitations and recommendation.

Concept checkYou want a portfolio project to show your skills. Which is the right choice?
Practitioner layer
  1. Pick a small, non-confidential dataset (for example a public retail dataset).
  2. Repeat the capstone steps and write a one-page report.
  3. Keep a short record of the question, method, findings and limitations.
  4. Ask someone to review your report and note their questions.
Expert layer

A portfolio shows judgement. Never publish a client’s real data. Use public or fictional data and say clearly that it is a practice project. Describe what you did, what you found and what you would do differently.

Check yourself: Why should you not put a client’s real data in your portfolio?

Answer: It breaks confidentiality and may break the law and your agreement. Use public or fictional data instead.

slides.title: Lock It In: Module Recap
slides.content:
1. Before You Start: Essential Business Language: Business analysis becomes easier when you understand the language used by business owners and managers.
  2. Business Problem 1: Selling More but Earning Less — Your Investigation: Where to begin: Start with sales transactions and product costs. Calculate revenue, COGS, gross profit and gross margin for each period. Then split the change by product. Check discounts, returns, supplier prices and sales mix.
  3. Business Problem 3: Rising Costs Eroding Profit — Your Investigation: Where to begin: Obtain the expense ledger, supplier invoices and budget. Group expenses into consistent categories. Compare the current period with the previous period and budget.
  4. Business Problem 5: Missed Growth Opportunities — Understand the Problem: What this means: Growth analysis looks for places where a business could serve more customers, sell more effectively or improve its offer.
  5. Business Problem 7: Unclear Business Performance — Understand the Problem: What this means: A business cannot manage performance consistently if it has no agreed measures, targets or reporting periods. A useful KPI has a clear definition, a reliable source, an owner and a reason for being monitored.
  6. Business Problem 8: Decisions Without Reliable Data — Your Investigation: Where to begin: Document the source of each field and KPI. Check row counts, missing values, duplicates, valid dates and numeric ranges. Reconcile totals against a trusted report or accounting record.
  7. Capstone: Investigate a Retail Business: Your assignment: A retail owner says: “We sell every day, but there is never enough money. Some products move quickly, others stay on the shelves, and I cannot tell which products actually make us money.”
  8. Where to Go Next: Turn Learning into Practice: You have completed the learning material when you can explain the eight business problems, calculate the basic measures, identify the records needed and communicate a defensible recommendation.
⭐ Activity: Close the lesson. Say each point above out loud in your own words, then give one example from your own life or work. Any point you cannot explain is where to go back and re-read.
Recall round (answer before you look)

Cover the answers. Say or write your answer to each question, then check yourself in the last layer below.

  1. A shop shows a KSh 150,000 profit but has no cash. Give one possible reason. (from: Before You Start: Essential Business Language)
  2. Why should you present stock value at cost, not at selling price? (from: Business Problem 2: Money Trapped in Slow-Moving Stock — Your Investigation)
  3. Why compare profit, not only revenue, between branches? (from: Business Problem 5: Missed Growth Opportunities — Understand the Problem)
  4. What makes a KPI useful? (from: Business Problem 7: Unclear Business Performance — Understand the Problem)
  5. A monthly report must refresh with new files each month without redoing the cleaning. Which tool helps most? (from: Choose the Right Tool for the Job)
  6. Why should you not put a client’s real data in your portfolio? (from: Where to Go Next: Turn Learning into Practice)
Teach it back
  1. Explain the three ideas you find hardest to a friend or family member in two minutes, without notes.
  2. Wherever you stumble, write the lesson name down and go back to it. Re-read the Practice layer and redo the activity.
  3. This week, use one idea from this module in real life or work, and note what happened.
  4. Come back in two days and answer the recall questions again. Remembering after a gap is what makes it stay.

Lessons to revisit if needed:

  • Before You Start: Essential Business Language
  • Business Problem 1: Selling More but Earning Less — Your Investigation
  • Business Problem 3: Rising Costs Eroding Profit — Your Investigation
  • Business Problem 5: Missed Growth Opportunities — Understand the Problem
  • Business Problem 7: Unclear Business Performance — Understand the Problem
  • Business Problem 8: Decisions Without Reliable Data — Your Investigation
  • Capstone: Investigate a Retail Business
  • Where to Go Next: Turn Learning into Practice
Check yourself: the answers

Answers, in the same order:

  1. Examples: customers have not paid yet, cash was spent on extra stock, a loan was repaid, or the owner withdrew money. Profit is not the same as cash.
  2. Cost shows the cash actually tied up. Selling price includes profit the business has not yet earned.
  3. A branch with lower revenue may have lower costs and more profit. Revenue alone hides this.
  4. A clear definition, a reliable data source, an owner and a target linked to a business goal.
  5. Power Query (in Excel or Power BI), because its recorded cleaning steps can be refreshed with new data.
  6. It breaks confidentiality and may break the law and your agreement. Use public or fictional data instead.

slides.title: What is a Capstone Project?
slides.content:
1. A capstone is your final, full-scale project that brings together all modules.
  2. It simulates a real-world data analysis task.
  3. You’ll choose a dataset, define a question, and present insights.
  4. It shows your skills in acquisition, cleaning, analysis, visualization, and presentation.
  5. It’s your portfolio centerpiece.
    6. Food for the Mind: A capstone isn’t just a task—it’s your proof of growth.
Practitioner layer

A capstone is one complete mini-project. Think of it as a short report with five parts: question, data, cleaning, analysis, recommendation. Example: "Which three products earn a duka the most profit?" Data: a month of sales with cost prices. Formula for each row: =(Price-Cost)*Qty. PivotTable by product, sort largest first, top three become the chart. Recommendation: keep these always in stock.

Check your idea with: can I finish it in a few weeks, is the data legal to use, and can I explain it to a non-expert in five minutes?

Expert layer

Scope is the main risk. A narrow, finished project beats an ambitious unfinished one. Write your question and stop rules at the start: what you will do and what you will leave out. Keep a project folder with raw data, cleaned data, analysis and notes, so another person could repeat your work. Be honest about limits and gaps. Real value comes from the decision your analysis supports. Learn next: pick the dataset and question as the next two slides explain.

Check yourself: What five parts should a finished capstone show?

Answer: A clear question, the data used, how it was cleaned, the analysis, and a recommendation or conclusion.

slides.title: Choosing Your Dataset
slides.content:
1. Pick a topic you care about: business, health, education, finance, etc.
  2. Use open data portals like Kaggle, Data.gov, or Kenya Open Data.
  3. Make sure the dataset is clean enough to work with, but rich enough to explore.
  4. Check for columns you can analyze and visualize.
  5. Save your source and document your choice.
    6. Food for the Mind: Choose data that speaks to you—your passion will power your project.
Practitioner layer

Dataset checklist, tested with a quick look:

  1. Source and licence: can I use and cite it?
  2. Size: at least a few hundred rows, so patterns are visible.
  3. Columns: at least one date or category, and one numeric measure.
  4. Quality: in Excel, filter each column and look for blanks; in pandas run df.isna().sum().
  5. Privacy: no names or ID numbers.

Example: county health facility counts from a public portal pass; a file of customer phone numbers does not. Write one paragraph recording why you chose it.

Expert layer

Picking data you care about helps motivation, but check the practicalities first. A dataset too clean teaches little; one that is too messy eats all your time. Open the file and attempt one chart before committing, since many portals hide problems in details. Read the metadata for definitions and units. Keep a note of the exact link and download date. If your first dataset fails, switching early is a good decision. Learn next: turn your dataset into a precise question.

Check yourself: Name three quick checks to run before committing to a dataset.

Answer: Check the source and licence, check column types and missing values, and check that it has no personal information. Try making one chart to confirm it is usable.

slides.title: Defining Your Question
slides.content:
1. Start with a clear, specific question.
  2. Examples: “Which region has the highest sales?” or “What factors affect student performance?”
  3. Break it into sub-questions if needed.
  4. Your question guides your entire analysis.
  5. Make sure it’s answerable with the data you have.
    6. Food for the Mind: A good question is half the answer—ask wisely.
Practitioner layer

Turning a topic into a question, step by step. Topic: shop sales.

  1. Vague: "Look at sales."
  2. Specific: "Which product category had the highest sales in each month?"
  3. Sub-questions: How many categories? Which month is highest? Is the pattern steady?
  4. Data check: do I have Date, Category and Amount?
  5. Answer shape: one table and one chart.

A test: can the question be answered with the columns I have, and would someone change a decision based on the answer? If not, rewrite it. Write it in one sentence at the top of your project.

Expert layer

Questions that start with "why" often need more data than you have; reframe as "what differs between..." and say what you can and cannot conclude. Avoid questions that hide an answer you want. Write what result would surprise you, then look for it honestly. Revise the question when the data shows its limits, and note the change. Keep it narrow: one main question and at most three sub-questions. Learn next: sketch the workflow that answers it.

Check yourself: Rewrite "analyse the clinic data" as a specific, answerable question.

Answer: For example: "Which clinic had the highest number of missed follow-up visits each quarter?" It names the measure, the unit and the time period, and can be answered with the data columns.

slides.title: Planning Your Workflow
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Import and clean your data.
  2. Step 2: Explore with summaries and visuals.
  3. Step 3: Build dashboards or reports.
  4. Step 4: Present findings with slides or notebooks.
  5. Step 5: Reflect and document your process.
    6. Food for the Mind: Plan your path—then walk it with purpose.
Practitioner layer

Turn the five steps into a dated checklist. Example for a two-week plan:

  1. Days 1-2 Import and clean: keep a raw copy, record every fix.
  2. Days 3-5 Explore: summaries (df.describe() or PivotTables), 3 to 5 quick charts.
  3. Days 6-8 Build: a dashboard or report answering the question.
  4. Days 9-11 Present: slides or notebook.
  5. Days 12-14 Reflect: test with a peer, document.

Add a daily 10-minute note: what I did, what is blocking me. Tick items as you finish.

Expert layer

Experts expect loops: exploration reveals dirty data, so you go back and clean again. That is normal, not failure. Keep each step reproducible, for example with a script or Power Query steps, so changes are easy to rerun. Leave time at the end, because presenting always takes longer than planned. If you run short, cut visuals, not checking. Write assumptions as you go rather than from memory. Learn next: choosing tools for each step.

Check yourself: Why should you keep a raw copy of the data before cleaning?
